Only `HtmlSanitizeEx.html5/1`, and custom scrubbers declared with `use HtmlSanitizeEx, extend: :html5`, permit `<style>` elements, and the sanitized output must be rendered to other users. Applications calling `HtmlSanitizeEx.Scrubber.CSS.scrub/1` directly are also affected.

summary: html_sanitize_ex HTML5 scrubber keeps attacker-supplied `<object>` elements, allowing untrusted content embedding
details:
## Summary

Inclusion of Functionality from Untrusted Control Sphere vulnerability in the HTML5 scrubber in rrrene html_sanitize_ex allows a remote attacker to load a document of their choosing into a trusted page via the `data` attribute of an `<object>` element in sanitized HTML. `object` is the one URI-bearing element in `lib/html_sanitize_ex/scrubber/html5.ex` never registered through `allow_tag_with_uri_attributes/3`, and its only guard is a prefix match on lowercase `"javascript:"`, so mixed-case variants, `data:` URIs, protocol-relative URLs and same-origin paths all survive.

This is not unconditional cross-site scripting. A `javascript:` URL does not execute through `<object data>` in current browsers, `data:` documents load in an opaque origin, and host-origin script execution additionally requires the application to serve attacker-controlled content from a same-origin path.

This issue affects html_sanitize_ex: from 0.3.1 before 1.4.5 and from 1.5.0-rc.0 before 1.5.3.

## Workarounds

Sanitize with `basic_html/1`, `markdown_html/1` or `strip_tags/1`, none of which allow `object`, or define a custom scrubber that omits it.

A Content-Security-Policy of `object-src 'none'` blocks an injected `<object>` from loading, and hosting user uploads on a separate origin removes the escalation path.

## Configurations

Only `HtmlSanitizeEx.html5/1`, and custom scrubbers declared with `use HtmlSanitizeEx, extend: :html5`, allow the `object` element, and the sanitized output must be rendered to other users.

Script execution in the host origin additionally requires the application to serve attacker-controlled HTML from a same-origin path, such as an uploads directory served as `text/html`.

summary: partisan decodes peer-plane frames with binary_to_term before authentication, allowing a remote VM abort
details:
## Summary

Deserialization of Untrusted Data vulnerability in lasp-lang partisan allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to abort the Erlang VM of a node via Excessive Allocation. `partisan_peer_service_server:handle_info/2` decodes every frame that arrives on the peer listener with `binary_to_term/1`, without the `safe` option, before `handle_inbound/2` interprets the message and before any peer authentication takes place. TLS is off by default and the listener accepts connections from any host, so one frame that names more atoms than the atom table holds aborts the VM. `partisan_peer_service_client:handle_info/2` decodes frames from the server side of a connection the same way.

The decode also materializes funs, ports and references the frame encodes and inflates compressed terms. The demonstrated impact is denial of service. partisan does not invoke decoded funs, so code execution was not shown.

This issue affects partisan: from 3.0.0 before 6.4.0.

## Details

**1. Listener.** `partisan_acceptor_socket` opens the peer port with `{packet, 4}` framing and a `packet_size` of `max_message_size` (64 MB by default). The cap bounds bytes per frame, not the term a frame decodes to. With `tls` unset the socket is plain TCP, and the listener binds to the node's host address unless `listen_addrs` says otherwise.

**2. Greeting.** `partisan_peer_service_server:acceptor_continue/3` accepts the socket, sends `{hello, Node}` unprompted and enters a `gen_server` loop. No cookie, shared secret or certificate check happens here.

**3. Unsafe decode.** The first frame reaches `partisan_peer_service_server:handle_info/2`, which calls `binary_to_term(Data)` with no `safe` option. The BIF interns every atom in the frame, builds every fun, port and reference, and inflates a compressed term, all before `handle_inbound/2` sees the result. A frame that names more atoms than the atom table holds aborts the VM at this step.

**4. Client side.** `partisan_peer_service_client:handle_info/2` decodes frames from the server end of a connection with the same call, so a node that connects to a hostile peer is exposed the same way.

**5. TLS.** Enabling `tls` wraps the socket but does not authenticate the peer unless both sides set `{verify, verify_peer}` with a cluster CA. Server-only TLS still lets any client that completes the handshake reach the decode.

## Proof of concept

1. Start partisan with its default configuration, so `tls` is `false`, and let the peer listener bind to `127.0.0.1:12345`.
2. From a plain TCP socket opened with `{packet, 4}`, send one frame holding the External Term Format of a list of 100,000 atoms the node has never seen (tag 131, `LIST_EXT`, 100,000 `SMALL_ATOM_UTF8_EXT` elements, `NIL_EXT`).
3. Read `erlang:system_info(atom_count)` before and after. The count rises by 100,001 and the sample atoms resolve with `binary_to_term(_, [safe])`, so the server interned them before any message interpretation or authentication. A frame naming more than 1,048,576 atoms, within the 64 MB default frame cap, aborts the VM.

## Impact

Any host that can open a TCP connection to the peer port stops the node with one frame, with no credentials and no cluster membership. The abort happens at VM level, so supervision trees cannot recover it, and every application running in that node goes down with partisan.

## Workarounds

Enable mutual TLS on the peer plane. Set `tls` to `true` and give `tls_server_options` a cluster CA in `cacertfile` together with `{verify, verify_peer}` and `{fail_if_no_peer_cert, true}`, and give `tls_client_options` the same CA with `{verify, verify_peer}`. The server then rejects a connection during the handshake unless the client presents a certificate the cluster CA issued, so the decode is only reachable by cluster members. Server-only TLS, or `verify_none`, does not help.

Where TLS cannot be enabled, restrict the peer listener port to trusted hosts with a host firewall or a private network segment.

## Solutions

The fixed release adds peer authentication and leaves it off by default (`peer_auth_methods` is `[]`). A node stays exposed until the option is set.

Set `peer_auth_methods` on every node to a list of `cryptosign`, `gossip_keyring` or `hmac_secret` without `anonymous`, with the trust material of each listed method (`peer_auth_cryptosign`, `peer_auth_keyring`, `peer_auth_secret`). The node then accepts only authentication frames of at most 4096 bytes from a peer that has not authenticated, and reads them without `binary_to_term/1`.

A node on an earlier release cannot connect to a node that requires authentication. Set the option on all nodes with `anonymous` at the end of the list, then remove `anonymous`. Peer authentication does not encrypt or sign later traffic, so use it over TLS 1.3 on a network that is not trusted.

summary: idna: punycode labels are decoded before the 63-octet length check, so a long xn-- label causes super-linear CPU use
details:
## Summary

Inefficient Algorithmic Complexity vulnerability in benoitc idna allows an attacker who controls a hostname passed to the library to exhaust CPU via an over-long `xn--` label. `idna:ulabel/1` in `src/idna.erl` hands every ASCII label that starts with `xn--` to `punycode:decode/1` without applying `check_label_length/1`, the 63-octet DNS label limit. `punycode:decode/1` in `src/punycode.erl` builds its output with list appends in `insert/4`, so its cost grows super-linearly with the label length. A label of a few kilobytes keeps a scheduler busy for seconds to minutes before the label is rejected as invalid punycode.

Every decode entry point reaches this path: `decode/1`, `decode/2`, `to_unicode/1` and `from_ascii/1`. The encode path reaches it as well, because `alabel/1` calls `ulabel/1` on an ASCII `xn--` label before its own length check, so `encode/1`, `encode/2` and `to_ascii/1` are affected for such input.

This issue affects idna: from 0.5.0 before 8.0.0.

## Details

**1. Label dispatch.** `idna:decode/2` in `src/idna.erl` lowercases the domain, splits it into labels and passes each one to `ulabel/1`. For an all-ASCII label that starts with `xn--`, `ulabel/1` strips the prefix and calls `punycode:decode/1` on the remainder. No length check runs before that call. `check_label_length/1`, which rejects labels longer than 63 octets, is only called from `alabel/1`, and there only after `alabel/1` has itself called `ulabel/1` on an ASCII label.

**2. Super-linear decoding.** `punycode:decode/1` in `src/punycode.erl` decodes one code point per delta and places it into the output with `insert/4`. `insert/4` walks to the insertion index by rebuilding the head with `Head ++ [C]` on every step and then appends the tail with another `++`. Each insertion therefore costs time quadratic in the insertion index, and the total work grows roughly with the cube of the label length. The reporter measured about an 8x increase in running time per doubling of the label.

**3. Work before rejection.** The crafted label is not valid punycode and the call eventually exits with an error, but only after the decoder has processed the whole label. The `?MAX` overflow guards in `punycode:decode/1` cover the RFC 3492 integer overflow class and do not bound the running time.

**4. Entry points.** `decode/1`, `decode/2`, `to_unicode/1` and `from_ascii/1` reach `ulabel/1` in every affected release. From 6.0.0, `alabel/1` calls `ulabel/1` on any ASCII label that starts with `xn--` before `check_label_length/1`, so `encode/1`, `encode/2`, `to_ascii/1` and `utf8_to_ascii/1` reach the decoder for such input as well.

## Proof of concept

1. Build an ASCII domain whose label is `xn--` followed by several thousand `a` characters and the digits `99`.
2. Call `idna:decode/1` on it and measure the call with `timer:tc/1`.
3. The call exits with an invalid punycode error only after the decoder has processed the whole label. The reporter measured on OTP 27: 506 bytes in 72 ms, 1006 bytes in 494 ms, 2006 bytes in 3.3 s and 4006 bytes in 27.2 s, about 8x per doubling.

## Impact

An attacker who can get an application to decode or encode a hostname they control, for example from a user-supplied URL or a redirect `Location` header, keeps one scheduler busy per call for seconds to hours depending on the label length. Enough concurrent calls exhaust the CPU of the VM.

## Workarounds

Before passing a hostname to idna, reject any domain that contains a label longer than 63 octets. The DNS limits labels to that length, so legitimate names pass unchanged, and the decoder never runs on the crafted label. The check must run before every call that reaches `idna:ulabel/1`, including `encode/1` and `to_ascii/1`, because `alabel/1` decodes an ASCII `xn--` label before checking its length.

summary: HTTP/2 request bodies made of 1-byte DATA frames amplify memory use in Bandit
details:
## Summary

Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling vulnerability in the HTTP/2 request body reader of mtrudel bandit allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to exhaust server memory via a request body sent as many 1-byte DATA frames.

`do_read_data/5` in `lib/bandit/http2/stream.ex` keeps every DATA frame payload as its own list element until the read returns. The `:length` option of `read_body/2` counts body bytes, not frames, so a body of 1-byte frames costs a list cell and a binary term per byte. Interleaving the frames across up to 500 concurrent streams per connection keeps each stream consuming its frames as they arrive; in the reporter's test, 100 streams held 25 to 40 MiB of stream process memory for 5 MB sent. Only routes whose Plug reads the request body are affected, which includes any route behind `Plug.Parsers`.

This issue affects bandit: from 0.3.1 before 1.14.1.

## Details

**1. Per-frame accumulation.** `Bandit.HTTP2.Stream.read_data/2` calls `do_read_data/5` in `lib/bandit/http2/stream.ex`, which prepends each `{:data, data, stream}` payload to a list (`[data | acc]`) and reverses it when the read returns. Each 1-byte payload arrives as a separate message from the connection process, so the stream heap holds a cons cell and a heap binary per frame.

**2. Byte-only limit.** `:length` (default 8,000,000) is decremented by `byte_size(data)` and bounds body bytes, not the number of frames. A read ends at `:length` or at its `read_timeout` deadline, and 1-byte frames add no measurable deadline credit, so a stream holds whatever arrives within the deadline at the per-frame overhead ratio. `Plug.Parsers` answers 413 on `:more`, and the client continues on a new stream.

**3. Interleaving defeats connection buffering.** The connection buffers DATA for a stream only once that stream has 16 messages outstanding. A stream that keeps up never reaches this, and interleaving one frame per stream per round across many streams keeps every stream under it regardless of TCP segment size.

**4. Measurements on 1.14.0.** 100 streams of 5,000 interleaved 1-byte frames (5,000,000 bytes on the wire, 488 KiB of body) held 25 to 40 MiB in stream processes, with empty mailboxes. One stream of 60,000 frames sent one per write held 2 to 4 MiB for 58 KiB of body.

## Proof of concept

1. Run Bandit with HTTP/2 enabled and a Plug that calls `Plug.Conn.read_body(conn)` with default options.
2. Open an h2c connection, exchange prefaces and SETTINGS, and send HEADERS for `POST /` without END_STREAM on 100 streams (IDs 1, 3, 5, ...).
3. Send 5,000 rounds of 1-byte DATA frames, one frame per stream per round, batched into writes of 100 frames.
4. Three seconds later, while the reads are still open, the 100 stream processes hold 25 to 40 MiB combined with empty mailboxes, for about 5 MB sent.

## Impact

An unauthenticated client can make a Bandit HTTP/2 server hold about 5 to 8 times the bytes it sends in stream process memory, across up to 500 streams per connection and many connections, for as long as each body read runs. This affects any Bandit server with HTTP/2 enabled whose routes read request bodies, which `Plug.Parsers` does for POST, PUT and PATCH.

## Workarounds

From 0.7.0, disable HTTP/2 with `http_2_options: [enabled: false]`, so that the vulnerable body reader never runs.

summary: jsv treats regex match budget exhaustion as a non-match, bypassing patternProperties and not
details:
## Summary

Improper Check for Unusual or Exceptional Conditions vulnerability in the `pattern` and `patternProperties` keywords in lud jsv allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to bypass schema validation via a string that matches a schema regex only after heavy backtracking. `JSV.Helpers.RegexExt.bounded_match?/2` runs schema regexes with a backtracking budget but calls `:re.run/3` without `:report_errors`, so a match that exhausts the budget returns the same `:nomatch` as a real non-match. A key that matches a `patternProperties` regex is then checked against `additionalProperties` or not at all, and a string that matches a `not` subschema with a `pattern` is accepted. Before the budget existed, `Regex.match?/2` failed the same way at Erlang's default match limit.

Only schemas whose regex explores a catastrophic branch before the branch that matches are affected. The attacker controls the data, not the schema, and linear patterns never exhaust the budget.

This issue affects jsv: from 0.1.0 before 0.26.2.

## Details

**1. Bounded matching.** `JSV.Helpers.RegexExt.bounded_match?/2` in `lib/jsv/helpers/regex_ext.ex` runs each schema regex through `:re.run/3` with `match_limit` and `match_limit_recursion` set to `10_000 + 50 * byte_size(subject)`, capped at 10,000,000. The call omits `:report_errors`, so PCRE's `match_limit` error is returned as `:nomatch`. The function compares the result to `:match` and returns `false` for a genuine non-match and for an exhausted budget alike.

**2. Keyword evaluation.** `JSV.Vocabulary.V202012.Validation.validate_keyword/3` uses the result for `pattern`, and `JSV.Vocabulary.V202012.Applicator` uses it to decide which `patternProperties` subschemas apply to each key. The draft 7 vocabulary delegates to the same modules. A `false` from an exhausted budget therefore means a `pattern` keyword fails and a `patternProperties` subschema is skipped.

**3. Inversion by combinators.** Under `not`, `anyOf`, `oneOf`, `if` and `contains`, a failing subschema can make the parent succeed, so a false non-match under `not` accepts a string the deny-list should reject. Under `patternProperties` the skipped subschema means the value is checked against `additionalProperties` or nothing.

**4. History.** Before the budget was introduced, the same keywords called `Regex.match?/2`, which also returns `false` on Erlang's default limit of 10,000,000 steps. The budget lowered the input size needed from about 25 bytes to about 20 bytes for the advisory's pattern.

## Proof of concept

1. Build a schema with `patternProperties` mapping the regex `^(?:(a+)+b|a+!)$` to `{"type": "integer"}`.
2. Submit an object whose only key is twenty `a` characters followed by `!` and whose value is the string `not an int`. The key matches the regex through its second alternative, but PCRE exhausts the 11,050-step budget in the first alternative.
3. `JSV.validate/2` returns `:ok`. The value is never checked against the subschema.
4. Build a second schema `{"not": {"pattern": "^(?:(a+)+b|a+!)$"}}` and submit the same string. `JSV.validate/2` returns `:ok` although the string matches the denied pattern.
5. Repeat with the short key `aaa!`. Both schemas now reject the data as expected.

## Impact

An attacker pads a string until its match exhausts the budget, so a value under a `patternProperties` key skips its subschema or a string passes a `not` deny-list. The application then accepts input its schema should reject.

## Workarounds

Pair `patternProperties` with `additionalProperties: false`. A key whose match exhausts the budget is then rejected instead of accepted unchecked. Valid keys that need heavy backtracking are rejected as well.

Write schema regexes without nested quantifiers or overlapping alternatives, and do not express deny-lists as a `not` subschema with a `pattern` on untrusted input.

## Configurations

The schema must contain a `pattern` or `patternProperties` regex that PCRE can match only after exploring a catastrophic branch first, such as a nested quantifier in an earlier alternative. Linear patterns never exhaust the budget. The attacker controls the validated data but not the schema.

summary: Cowboy HTTP/1.1 Unbounded Buffering of Pipelined Data During Request Handling Enables Memory Exhaustion
details:
## Summary

Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling vulnerability in ninenines cowboy allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to exhaust connection process memory over HTTP/1.1.

Once a request has been received in full and its handler is still running, `cowboy_http:parse/2` in `src/cowboy_http.erl` appends every further byte that arrives on the keep-alive connection to the connection buffer and returns to the receive loop without parsing it. The socket stays in active mode and no limit applies to this buffer: `max_request_line_length`, `max_headers` and the other parser limits only take effect once the handler returns and parsing resumes, and the only timer in this state is `idle_timeout` (default 60 seconds), which is reset on every received chunk. A client can therefore send an arbitrary amount of data on one connection for as long as the handler runs, and a few connections to an endpoint that holds requests open can drive the Erlang VM into out-of-memory conditions.

This issue affects cowboy: from 2.18.0 before 2.21.0.

## Details

**1. Request completes, handler runs.** When `cowboy_http` finishes reading a request it moves the parser to the `ps_next_request` state while the stream for that request is still alive. The connection process keeps the socket in active mode (`setopts_active/1` re-arms `{active, N}` whenever a passive notification arrives), so the VM continues to deliver socket data to the process.

**2. Data is appended, never parsed.** Each incoming chunk reaches `loop/1`, which concatenates it onto the connection buffer and calls `parse/2`. The `parse/2` clause for `in_state=ps_next_request` with a live `#stream{}` returns straight to `before_loop/1` with the enlarged buffer, deferring all parsing until the current stream stops. The parser limits (`max_request_line_length`, `max_header_name_length`, `max_header_value_length`, `max_headers`) are enforced only by the parsing clauses that run after that point, and `max_skip_body_length` only covers an unread body of the current request, not bytes after it.

**3. No timer bounds the window.** While a stream is live the connection runs on `idle_timeout` (default 60 seconds), and `set_timeout/2` resets it on every received chunk. The attacker therefore keeps the window open by continuing to send. Only the handler finishing ends it, at which point parsing resumes, the buffered bytes fail the request-line checks, and the connection closes with a 4xx response. By then the data has been held for the full handler duration.

**4. Introduction.** The behaviour arrived with the change that removed concurrent processing of pipelined HTTP/1.1 requests (first shipped in 2.18.0). Earlier releases parsed pipelined data as it arrived, so excess bytes hit the request-line limit immediately and the connection was closed with `414 Request-URI Too Long` before any significant amount was buffered. The introducing commit describes the intended behaviour as stopping reads from the socket until the stream stops, but the code keeps the socket active and buffers instead.

## Proof of concept

1. Start a cowboy HTTP/1.1 listener with a handler that takes time to reply, for example one that sleeps 20 seconds before calling `cowboy_req:reply/4`.
2. Open one TCP connection and send a complete `GET / HTTP/1.1` request with a `Host` header.
3. While the handler is still running, keep writing arbitrary bytes on the same connection, for example 300 one-megabyte chunks.
4. Inspect the connection process with `erlang:process_info/2` while the handler runs: its referenced binaries grow by the amount sent and `erlang:memory(binary)` rises by the same amount. No parser limit or timeout interrupts the transfer.
5. When the handler replies, the client still receives the `200 OK`; only afterwards does the buffered data get parsed and rejected.

On 2.16.1 and 2.17.0 step 3 is cut short: the server answers `414 Request-URI Too Long` with `connection: close` as soon as the first chunk arrives and holds nothing.

## Impact

An unauthenticated remote client can make one connection process hold an arbitrary amount of memory by sending data after a request while its handler runs. A few such connections to an endpoint that holds requests open exhaust node memory and terminate every connection served by that node.

## Configurations

The amount of data buffered scales with how long the current handler keeps the connection busy. Any HTTP/1.1 endpoint exposes a window, but deployments with handlers that hold a request open, such as long polling with `cowboy_loop`, streamed responses via `cowboy_req:stream_reply/3`, or slow backend calls, give an attacker the time to buffer significant memory. HTTP/2 connections are not affected.

summary: Unbounded query cache growth from interpolated JSON paths and splice lists in Ecto
details:
## Summary

Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling vulnerability in elixir-ecto ecto allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to exhaust memory in the application and in the database server by sending requests with distinct JSON keys or list lengths where the application interpolates them into `json_extract_path/2`, `field[^key]` or `splice/1`. Ecto caches prepared queries per repository in an ETS table with no size limit and no eviction. Interpolated JSON path elements become part of the query expression instead of its parameters, and `splice/1` expands into one placeholder per element, so every distinct key or list length creates a new cache entry. With ecto_sql each entry is also a new prepared statement on the database connection that runs it. None of this memory is released until the processes restart.

This issue affects ecto: from 3.4.0 before 3.14.3.

## Details

**1. Cache keys** (`lib/ecto/query/builder.ex`, `lib/ecto/query/planner.ex`)

`escape_json_path/2` checks interpolated path elements with `json_path_element!/1`, and a whole interpolated path with `json_path!/1`, at runtime and places the resulting strings and integers in the `{:json_extract_path, [], [field, path]}` expression instead of in the query parameters. `Ecto.Query.Planner` builds the cache key from the query expressions, so every distinct path is a distinct key. `splice(^list)` keeps the values as parameters but expands into one placeholder per element. `cast_and_merge_params/5` marks `{:in, _}` parameters as not cacheable but keeps `{:splice, _}` parameters cacheable, so every distinct list length is a distinct key, and the entry grows with the length.

**2. Cache storage** (`lib/ecto/query/planner.ex`, `lib/ecto/repo/supervisor.ex`)

`Ecto.Query.Planner.query/6` stores each new query with `:ets.insert_new/2` in the table that `Ecto.Repo.Supervisor` creates with `new_query_cache/1`, and nothing removes entries. ecto_sql renders the path into the SQL text, for example `WHERE ((i0."meta"#>array['color']::text[]) = $1)`, and Postgrex prepares a named statement for each new SQL text on the connection that runs it.

**3. Effect**

Each request with a new key or list length adds memory that is never released, in the BEAM, where the cache is shared by the whole repository, and with ecto_sql in the database server, where prepared statements are kept per connection. Large keys amplify this: every 1 MB of request data retained about 2 MB in the application and 3 MB in PostgreSQL. The query cache was disabled for `values/2` sources after a similar report, but not for these two cases.

## Proof of concept

Reproduced on Ecto main (`ad8fda5`) with ecto_sql 3.14.0, Postgrex 0.22.4 and PostgreSQL 18.4, on Elixir 1.20.4 and Erlang/OTP 29, with `pool_size: 1`.

1. Define a handler that filters by a JSON key from the request: `Repo.all(from i in Item, where: json_extract_path(i.meta, ^[key]) == ^value, select: i.id)`.
2. Send 2,000 requests with the same key. The query cache has 1 entry and the connection 1 prepared statement; PostgreSQL backend memory goes from 2 MB to 3 MB.
3. Send 2,000 more requests with distinct short keys. The cache has 2,001 entries and the connection 2,001 prepared statements; backend memory is 21 MB.
4. Send 200 requests with a distinct 500 KB key each (100 MB in total). BEAM binary memory grows by 191 MB and PostgreSQL backend memory by 289 MB, measured after garbage collecting every process.
5. Repeating a key that was already seen adds nothing. `fragment("? IN (?)", i.id, splice(^ids))` with list lengths 1 to 300 adds 300 cache entries, while `i.id in ^ids` with the same lengths adds 1.

## Impact

An unauthenticated client can make the application and its database keep memory from every request that carries a new JSON key or list length, when the application passes it into an interpolated JSON path or `splice/1`. Nothing frees that memory until the processes restart. In the proof of concept, 200 requests with 100 MB of keys in total left 191 MB in the BEAM and 289 MB in the PostgreSQL backend of one connection. Sustained requests exhaust memory in the application node, the database server, or both.

## Workarounds

Pass the path as a query parameter so it is not part of the cache key. With PostgreSQL: `fragment("? #> ?", i.meta, type(^path, {:array, :string}))`. Alternatively, disable the cache for these queries with `Repo.all(query, query_cache: false)`, or restrict keys and list lengths to a known set before building the query.

## Configurations

The application must pass request data into an interpolated JSON path (`json_extract_path(field, ^path)`, `json_extract_path(field, [^key])` or `field[^key]`), or a request-controlled list into `splice/1`, and run the query through a repository with the default `query_cache: true`.

## Solutions

Upgrade Ecto to 3.14.3 or later. Queries with interpolated JSON path elements or an interpolated `splice/1` list are no longer cached, the same as running them with `query_cache: false`, so distinct keys and list lengths don't add cache entries.

summary: Phoenix.HTML vulnerable to attribute injection via unvalidated attribute names in attributes_escape/1
details:
## Summary

Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation ('Cross-site Scripting') vulnerability in phoenixframework phoenix_html allows an attacker who controls attribute names to inject attributes and script into rendered HTML via `Phoenix.HTML.attributes_escape/1`.

`attributes_escape/1` in `lib/phoenix_html.ex` escapes attribute values but not attribute names. `key_escape/1` passes a binary key through `html_escape`, which neutralizes quotes and angle brackets but not whitespace, so a key such as `x onmouseover` ends the attribute and starts a new one. An atom key is only dasherized, so any character passes, including quotes and `>`. Nested `data`, `aria` and `phx` keys take the same paths. An application is affected when it builds attribute keys from untrusted input and renders them through HEEx `<tag {@attrs}>`, `content_tag/3`, or a direct call. Before 3.0.0 the same code lived in `Phoenix.HTML.Tag`.

This issue affects phoenix_html: from 1.0.0 before 3.3.5 and from 4.0.0 before 4.4.0.

## Details

**1. Attribute rendering.** `Phoenix.HTML.attributes_escape/1` walks the key-value pairs through `build_attrs/1` and `nested_attrs/3` and emits each as `key_escape(k)="attr_escape(v)"`. Values are escaped. Names are not checked against the HTML attribute-name grammar.

**2. Binary names.** `key_escape/1` sends a binary through `Phoenix.HTML.Engine.html_escape/1`, which replaces `&`, `<`, `>`, `"` and `'`. Whitespace passes. HTML uses whitespace to separate attributes, so `%{"x onmouseover" => "alert(1)"}` renders ` x onmouseover="alert(1)"`: a harmless `x` attribute followed by an attacker-chosen event handler.

**3. Atom names.** `key_escape/1` converts an atom with `Atom.to_string/1` and replaces `_` with `-`. Nothing is escaped, so `[{:"x\" onclick=\"alert(1)", "y"}]` renders ` x" onclick="alert(1)="y"` and `aria: [{:"x\"><script>", "y"}]` renders ` aria-x"><script>="y"`, which leaves the tag entirely. This path needs the application to create atoms from untrusted input, for example `Jason.decode!(body, keys: :atoms)` or `String.to_atom/1` on a parameter.

**4. Reachability.** HEEx compiles `<div {@attrs}>` to a call to `Phoenix.HTML.attributes_escape/1` through `Phoenix.LiveView.HTMLEngine` and `Phoenix.LiveView.TagEngine`. `tag/2` and `content_tag/3` in `Phoenix.HTML.Tag` (phoenix_html 1.x to 3.x) and in `PhoenixHTMLHelpers.Tag` (4.x) render attributes the same way. Versions before 3.0.0 emitted the dasherized name without any escaping at all.

## Proof of concept

1. Install a vulnerable release, for example `Mix.install([{:phoenix_html, "== 4.3.0"}])`.
2. Render a binary name containing a space: `Phoenix.HTML.attributes_escape(%{"x onmouseover" => "alert(1)"}) |> Phoenix.HTML.safe_to_string()` returns ` x onmouseover="alert(1)"`.
3. Render an atom name containing a quote: `Phoenix.HTML.attributes_escape([{:"x\" onclick=\"alert(1)", "y"}]) |> Phoenix.HTML.safe_to_string()` returns ` x" onclick="alert(1)="y"`.
4. Render a nested atom name: `Phoenix.HTML.attributes_escape(aria: [{:"x\"><script>", "y"}]) |> Phoenix.HTML.safe_to_string()` returns ` aria-x"><script>="y"`.
5. Place any of these maps in a HEEx template as `<div {@attrs}>` to deliver the injected attribute to a browser.

## Impact

An attacker who can influence the attribute names an application renders can add event-handler attributes or close the tag and run script in the browser of every user who views the page.

## Workarounds

Do not derive attribute names from untrusted input. Where dynamic attribute keys are needed, check each key against an allow list, or against a pattern such as `^[a-zA-Z][a-zA-Z0-9:._-]*$`, before passing the map to `attributes_escape/1` or a HEEx `{@attrs}` expression. Do not create atoms from request data.

summary: AshAuthentication TOTP setup lets a user install their own authenticator secret on another user's account
details:
## Summary

Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key vulnerability in team-alembic ash_authentication allows a user with an account to install a TOTP secret they control on another user's account, and then sign in as that user or hold their second factor.

`AshAuthentication.Strategy.Totp.ConfirmSetupChange` verified a setup token but did not check that it was issued to the record being confirmed, so an attacker's own pending secret could be confirmed onto another user's record. The TOTP setup changes, `ConfirmSetupChange`, `GeneratePendingSetupChange` and `GenerateSecretChange`, also marked their changesets as AshAuthentication interactions, which the standard `AshAuthenticationInteraction` policy bypass lets through. A policy limiting `setup` and `confirm_setup` to the actor's own record therefore never ran when an application exposed those actions by record key, and a direct `setup` call on another user's record returned that user's pending secret and setup token.

This issue affects ash_authentication: from 5.0.0-rc.0 before 5.0.0-rc.16.

## Workarounds

Do not expose `setup` or `confirm_setup` on a record the caller chooses. Call them through `AshAuthentication.Strategy.Totp.Actions` with the signed-in user, as the built-in routes do.

## Configurations

An application exposes the TOTP `setup` or `confirm_setup` action on a record the caller identifies, for example through AshJsonApi, AshGraphql or a controller that passes a looked-up user to `AshAuthentication.Strategy.Totp.Actions.confirm_setup/3`, and the attacker can read the victim's user record. Installing the attacker's secret requires `confirm_setup_enabled? true`; signing in with it alone requires `sign_in_enabled? true`. The routes AshAuthentication and AshAuthenticationPhoenix provide always use the signed-in user and are not affected.

summary: ssl_verify_fun: partial-label wildcard certificate matches hostnames across a label boundary
details:
## Summary

Improper Validation of Certificate with Host Mismatch vulnerability in deadtrickster ssl_verify_fun allows an adversary in the middle to impersonate a TLS peer via a certificate that carries a partial-label wildcard. `try_match_wildcard/4` in `src/ssl_verify_hostname.erl` anchors only the text before and after the `*` of an identifier such as `f*.example.net`, so the wildcard also consumes dots and the certificate is accepted for `f.evil.example.net`. RFC 6125 confines a wildcard to the left-most label. The same matcher lets `*.168.1.1` match the IP literal `192.168.1.1`. Whole-label wildcards are matched correctly.

Erlang/OTP 20.0 and later check the hostname in `ssl` before a user `verify_fun` sees `valid_peer`, so a client that keeps `server_name_indication` set rejects the mismatch regardless. Exposed are clients that disable SNI, servers that verify client certificate hostnames with this library, and direct callers of `verify_cert_hostname/2`.

This issue affects ssl_verify_fun: from 1.0.1 before 1.1.8.

## Details

**1. Identifier parsing.** `ssl_verify_hostname:try_match_hostname/2` strips trailing dots, tries an exact case-insensitive match, and otherwise calls `parse_and_validate_wildcard_identifier/2`. That function accepts an identifier with one `*` in the left-most label and at least two labels after it, and classifies it as `SingleCharW` when the label is exactly `*`.

**2. Whole-label wildcard, correct.** For `*.example.net` the matcher compares the text after the `*` with the hostname from its first dot onward, so `a.b.example.net` fails because `.b.example.net` differs from `.example.net`.

**3. Partial-label wildcard, incorrect.** For `f*.example.net` the `SingleCharW` branch is skipped. `try_match_wildcard/4` then checks only that the hostname ends with `.example.net` and starts with `f`. Nothing checks the span consumed by the `*`, so `f.evil.example.net` and `f.a.b.example.net` pass. RFC 6125 section 6.4.3 limits a wildcard to the left-most label. The `wildcard_not_in_a_label/2` guard only rejects internationalized `xn--` labels and does not help.

**4. IP literals.** The reference identifier is treated as a DNS name whatever its shape, so `verify_cert_hostname/2` with hostname `192.168.1.1` matches a `dNSName` of `*.168.1.1` through the whole-label branch. RFC 6125 does not apply wildcard matching to IP addresses, and OTP's `ssl` converts an IP-literal string to an `{ip, ...}` reference that only matches `iPAddress` entries.

**5. Interaction with Erlang/OTP.** When `ssl_verify_hostname:verify_fun/3` is used as `verify_fun`, OTP 20.0 and later call `ssl_certificate:validate/4` for `valid_peer` before the user fun. In the client role with `server_name_indication` set to a hostname, or with a peer IP from a socket upgrade, OTP runs `public_key:pkix_verify_hostname/3` and hands the user fun `{bad_cert, hostname_check_failed}` instead of `valid_peer`, which ssl_verify_fun turns into `{fail, ...}`. OTP's default match function allows no wildcards, and its `https` match function (`public_key:pkix_verify_hostname_match_fun/1`) splits both names on dots and matches the wildcard within the first label only. The ssl_verify_fun result therefore decides the outcome only with `{server_name_indication, disable}`, in the server role, on direct calls to `verify_cert_hostname/2`, or on OTP older than 20.0.

## Proof of concept

1. Issue a leaf certificate whose only `subjectAltName` entry is `dNSName` `f*.example.net`, for example with `public_key:pkix_test_data/1`, and decode it with `public_key:pkix_decode_cert(Der, otp)`.
2. Call `ssl_verify_hostname:verify_cert_hostname(Cert, "foo.example.net")`. It returns `{valid, "foo.example.net"}`, as expected.
3. Call `ssl_verify_hostname:verify_cert_hostname(Cert, "f.evil.example.net")`. It returns `{valid, "f.evil.example.net"}` although the hostname spans two labels where the wildcard sits.
4. Call `ssl_verify_hostname:verify_cert_hostname(Cert, "a.b.example.net")` as a control. It returns `{fail, unable_to_match_altnames}`.
5. For the IP-literal variant, issue a leaf with `dNSName` `*.168.1.1` and call `verify_cert_hostname(Cert, "192.168.1.1")`. It returns `{valid, "192.168.1.1"}`.
6. To observe the full TLS path, serve the first certificate from `ssl:listen/2` and connect with `{verify, verify_peer}`, the CA in `cacerts`, `{verify_fun, {fun ssl_verify_hostname:verify_fun/3, [{check_hostname, "f.evil.example.net"}]}}` and `{server_name_indication, disable}`. The handshake succeeds. With `{server_name_indication, "f.evil.example.net"}` instead, OTP 20.0 or later rejects the certificate with `hostname_check_failed` before ssl_verify_fun runs.

## Impact

A holder of a certificate for `f*.example.net` from a CA the client trusts can impersonate any host named `f.<label>.example.net` to a client that relies on ssl_verify_fun alone for hostname verification, and read or alter the traffic of that connection.

## Workarounds

On Erlang/OTP 21 or later, keep `server_name_indication` set to the target hostname and pass `{customize_hostname_check, [{match_fun, public_key:pkix_verify_hostname_match_fun(https)}]}` in the `ssl` options. The hostname check in `ssl` then rejects the mismatch before ssl_verify_fun runs, and legitimate wildcard certificates continue to match. hackney and tls_certificate_check already set both options.

## Configurations

ssl_verify_fun decides the outcome only where it is the sole hostname check. Erlang/OTP 20.0 and later verify the hostname in `ssl` before the user `verify_fun` is called with `valid_peer`, as long as `server_name_indication` is a hostname or the connection was upgraded from a socket. A deployment is exposed when it sets `{server_name_indication, disable}`, when a TLS server uses `ssl_verify_hostname:verify_fun/3` to verify client certificates, when it calls `ssl_verify_hostname:verify_cert_hostname/2` directly, or when it runs Erlang/OTP older than 20.0. The attacker also needs a certificate with a partial-label wildcard from a CA the client trusts, which the CA/Browser Forum Baseline Requirements do not allow, so the realistic exposure is private PKI.

summary: Unbounded decoded HTTP/2 header-list size in cowlib cow_http2_machine enables HPACK amplification memory exhaustion
details:
## Summary

Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling vulnerability in ninenines cowlib allows an unauthenticated remote peer to exhaust the memory of an HTTP/2 endpoint via HPACK-indexed header fields.

`cow_http2_machine:headers_decode/4` in `src/cow_http2_machine.erl` decodes every HEADERS block with `cow_hpack:decode/3`. It bounds the compressed block size and the number of fields, but not the size of the decoded header list that RFC 9113 section 6.5.2 places under `SETTINGS_MAX_HEADER_LIST_SIZE`. A peer stores one header value of up to the dynamic table size (4096 bytes by default) and then references it with one-byte indexed fields, so about 100 bytes on the wire decode to a header list of about 390 KB. A consumer that copies the decoded values, as Cowboy does when `cowboy_http2:headers_to_map/2` joins repeated `cookie` fields into one binary, allocates that amount for every stream. The total across streams and connections is not bounded.

This issue affects cowlib: from 2.7.0 before 2.22.0.

## Details

**1. The decoder bounds everything but the decoded size.** `cow_http2_machine:headers_decode/4` passes each complete header block to `cow_hpack:decode/3`. Two limits apply: `max_fragmented_header_block_size` (32768 bytes by default) on the compressed block, and `max_headers` (100 by default, added in cowlib 2.17.0) on the number of fields. `max_header_list_size` appears in the module's option list with a default of `infinity`, next to a `@todo` comment, and is neither advertised in SETTINGS nor enforced on the decoded list, which is what RFC 9113 section 6.5.2 defines it for.

**2. One-byte fields expand to kilobytes.** The dynamic table holds entries of up to `max_decode_table_size` (4096 bytes by default). The peer sends one literal field with incremental indexing carrying a 4000-byte value, which becomes table entry 62. Every later field is the single byte `0xBE`, an indexed representation of that entry. A 110-byte block that carries four pseudo-headers and 96 such references decodes to a 100-field list whose values total 384,000 bytes. Before 2.17.0 no field count applied, so a 32 KB block referenced the entry about 32,000 times.

**3. The allocation is realised by the consumer.** The list that `cow_hpack` returns is cheap, about 2 KB of heap, because every reference shares the one table binary. Cowboy's `cowboy_http2:headers_to_map/2` joins repeated fields into a single new binary (`"; "` for `cookie`, `", "` for other names), so each stream yields a 384,190-byte cookie value that lives in the request process for the life of the stream. Cowboy's HTTP/1.1 limits `max_header_value_length` and `max_headers` do not apply to HTTP/2. With the default `max_concurrent_streams` of 100 a connection holds about 38 MB, and only the Ranch connection limit bounds the total. Gun hands the decoded list to the owner process without copying the values, so the client side sees a small list per response and no amplification.

**4. Measurement.** On cowboy 2.20.0 with cowlib 2.21.0 on Erlang/OTP 29, one h2c connection on loopback sent 15,943 bytes of HEADERS for 100 streams. Binary memory grew by 38.4 MB and every handler received a 384,190-byte `cookie` header. A control with the same 100 streams and no indexed fields grew by 0.

## Proof of concept

1. Start a Cowboy clear listener with default protocol options and a handler that takes a few seconds to reply, so streams stay open.
2. Open one TCP connection, send the HTTP/2 client preface and an empty SETTINGS frame.
3. On stream 1 send a HEADERS frame with `END_HEADERS` and `END_STREAM` whose block contains `:method`, `:scheme`, `:path` and `:authority`, then one literal `cookie` field with incremental indexing carrying a 4000-byte value, then 95 indexed fields `0xBE` referencing it.
4. On streams 3 through 199 send the same frame with the four pseudo-headers followed by 96 indexed fields `0xBE`. Each block is 110 bytes.
5. Watch `erlang:memory(binary)` on the server. It grows by about 38 MB for about 16 KB sent, and `cowboy_req:header(<<"cookie">>, Req)` in each handler returns a 384,190-byte binary.

## Impact

A remote unauthenticated client makes an HTTP/2 server built on cowlib, such as a Cowboy listener, allocate roughly 2,400 times the bytes it sends. One connection reaches about 38 MB with default settings, and an attacker holding many connections can drive the Erlang VM out of memory.

## Workarounds

Cowboy servers that do not need HTTP/2 can set `protocols => [http]` in the protocol options. The listener then answers the HTTP/2 preface with `501 Not Implemented` and the decoder is never reached.

Lowering `max_headers` in the HTTP/2 protocol options shrinks the per-stream allocation in proportion, to about `max_headers` times the 4096-byte table entry. This reduces the amplification but does not remove it.

summary: AshAuthentication brute_force_strategy does not limit sign-in and request actions defined on the resource
details:
## Summary

Improper Restriction of Excessive Authentication Attempts vulnerability in team-alembic ash_authentication allows an unauthenticated attacker to guess passwords and one-time passwords without limit.

The password, magic link and OTP strategies enforce `brute_force_strategy` by adding a preparation only to the actions they generate. When the resource defines one of those actions itself, the strategy uses it as written and nothing checked that it carried the preparation, so the setting compiled and applied no limit. The generators produce exactly this: `mix ash_authentication.install` writes `sign_in_with_password`, `request_password_reset_token` and `request_magic_link`, `mix ash_authentication.upgrade` then adds `brute_force_strategy` to those strategies, and `mix ash_authentication.add_strategy.otp` writes its OTP actions without the preparation. Separately, with `registration_enabled? true` the OTP sign-in is a create action, which preparations do not run on, so `brute_force_strategy {:preparation, module}` never applied to it.

This issue affects ash_authentication: from 5.0.0-rc.4 before 5.0.0-rc.16.

## Workarounds

Add the brute-force preparation to each protected action defined on the resource, or remove the action so the strategy generates it. For `brute_force_strategy {:audit_log, name}` that is `prepare {AshAuthentication.AddOn.AuditLog.IdentityBruteForcePreparation, action_name: <action>}` on the password sign-in, password reset request, magic link request and OTP request actions, and `prepare {AshAuthentication.AddOn.AuditLog.BruteForcePreparation, action_name: <action>}` on a read OTP sign-in action. For `{:preparation, MyModule}` it is `prepare MyModule`. For OTP with `registration_enabled? true`, switch to `brute_force_strategy :rate_limit`.

## Configurations

A password, magic link or OTP strategy sets `brute_force_strategy` and one of its protected actions (password sign-in, password reset request, magic link request, OTP sign-in or OTP request) is defined on the resource without the matching brute-force preparation, as on resources set up by the installer, the upgrade task or the OTP generator. Alternatively, an OTP strategy sets `registration_enabled? true` with `brute_force_strategy {:preparation, module}`. Actions the strategies generate themselves, and the OTP strategy's `:rate_limit` mode, are not affected.

summary: HTTP/2 StreamError recovery rolls back connection state and bypasses per-connection limits in Bandit
details:
## Summary

Improper Cleanup on Thrown Exception vulnerability in the HTTP/2 handler of mtrudel bandit allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to bypass per-connection resource limits via a single TCP write that carries several frames, one of which raises a stream error.

When a frame raises `StreamError` partway through a chunk, `Bandit.HTTP2.Handler.handle_data/3` sends RST_STREAM and continues with the connection state from before the chunk, dropping the rest of it. Streams opened by earlier frames in the chunk keep running their Plug calls, but the stream counts, `last_stream_id`, the rapid-reset timestamps, the HPACK decoder state and the buffer roll back, so `max_concurrent_streams`, `max_requests` and the rapid-reset limiter never see those streams. A client that sends one HEADERS frame more than `max_concurrent_streams` in each write has the extra refused and the others forgotten: with a limit of 10, five such writes run 50 Plug calls at once.

This issue affects bandit: from 1.9.0 before 1.14.0.

## Details

**1. Function-level rescue.** `Bandit.HTTP2.Handler.handle_data/3` in `lib/bandit/http2/handler.ex` deserializes every frame in a TCP chunk inside an `Enum.reduce_while/3` and wraps the whole function in a `rescue`. Inside that `rescue`, `state` is the original function argument, not the `reduce_while` accumulator.

**2. Rollback on StreamError.** When `Bandit.HTTP2.Connection.handle_frame/3` raises `StreamError` partway through the chunk, `rescue_stream_error/3` sends RST_STREAM and returns `{:continue, state}` with the connection as it was before the chunk. The rest of the chunk is dropped.

**3. Lost bookkeeping.** Frames already handled keep their side effects: their stream processes are running the Plug. But the stream counts, `last_stream_id`, `reset_stream_timestamps`, `recv_hpack_state` and `buffer` are rolled back, so `max_concurrent_streams`, `max_requests` and the rapid-reset limiter no longer count those streams. The same rollback drops HPACK table updates, which can mix up headers between requests, misaligns frame parsing, and sends a stale `last_stream_id` in GOAWAY.

## Proof of concept

1. Run Bandit with a Plug that blocks until released and with `http_2_options: [default_local_settings: [max_concurrent_streams: 10]]`.
2. Open an HTTP/2 connection with prior knowledge and complete the SETTINGS exchange.
3. In one TCP write, send 11 HEADERS frames with END_HEADERS and END_STREAM on streams 1, 3, ..., 21, each carrying a header block encoded without indexing. The eleventh is refused with REFUSED_STREAM, and the server forgets the ten streams before it.
4. Send the same write four more times. The Plug runs 50 times concurrently against a limit of 10.

## Impact

An unauthenticated client can run more concurrent Plug calls on one HTTP/2 connection than the configured `max_concurrent_streams` allows (five times the limit in the reporter's test), tying up the server processes, CPU and memory the limit is meant to cap. Servers that serve HTTP/2 with a finite `max_concurrent_streams` are affected.

## Workarounds

Disable HTTP/2 with `http_2_options: [enabled: false]`, so that the vulnerable HTTP/2 handler never runs.

summary: Ash.count, Ash.exists and Ash.aggregate skip related resources' read policies in filters and sorts
details:
## Summary

Incorrect Authorization vulnerability in ash-project ash allows an actor to infer data in related records they cannot read via `Ash.count/2`, `Ash.exists/2` and `Ash.aggregate/3`.

`Ash.Actions.Aggregate.run/4` (`lib/ash/actions/aggregate.ex`) applied only the root resource's read policy before running the aggregate query. The read path also applies each related resource's read policy to filter and sort references that cross a relationship, directly (for example `comments.body`) or through an aggregate over one, but the aggregate path skipped that step. A caller whose filter or sort reaches these functions, for example through `Ash.Query.filter_input/2`, an ash_lua script, or an AshAi tool offering count or exists results, can test conditions against related rows hidden from them and recover their existence and attribute values one query at a time. `Ash.read/2` and its page counts are not affected.

This issue affects ash: from 2.6.0 before 3.34.6.

## Configurations

Reachable only when an application passes caller-supplied filters or sorts that cross a relationship into `Ash.count/2`, `Ash.exists/2` or `Ash.aggregate/3` (directly, through ash_lua read operations, or through AshAi count, exists or aggregate result types), and a related resource's read policy is stricter than the root resource's.

summary: WebSocket 1-byte continuation frames bypass `max_fragmented_message_size` in Bandit
details:
## Summary

Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling vulnerability in the WebSocket fragment reassembly of mtrudel bandit allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to exhaust server memory via a fragmented message made of many 1-byte continuation frames.

`Bandit.WebSocket.Connection` checks `max_fragmented_message_size` against the payload bytes received, but keeps every non-final continuation frame as a new list cell around its own binary, and nothing limits the number of fragments. A 1-byte fragment costs 7 bytes on the wire but about 150 to 170 bytes of server memory, so one connection can hold about 150 times the configured limit, roughly 1.2 to 1.4 GB at the default 8 MB. Ping frames between fragments keep the connection alive past the idle timeout.

This issue affects bandit: from 1.11.0 before 1.14.0.

## Details

**1. Byte-only limit.** In `Bandit.WebSocket.Connection` (`lib/bandit/websocket/connection.ex`), the fragment limit is checked against `fragment_size`, which only adds up payload bytes (`IO.iodata_length(frame.data)`).

**2. Per-fragment accumulation.** Each non-final continuation frame is stored as a new cons cell around its own binary, `[connection.fragment_frame.data | frame.data]`. Only zero-length fragments are kept out, so 1-byte fragments are accepted. Each costs 7 bytes on the wire but keeps about 150 to 170 bytes in memory. Against 1.12.5, 1M fragments kept about 169 MB and 3M kept about 450 MB, growing linearly, and about 56 MB of traffic reaches the 8 MB payload cap.

**3. Kept alive.** Ping frames sent between fragments are handled by `handle_control_frame` without touching the fragment state, so they keep the connection alive past the idle timeout.

## Proof of concept

1. Run Bandit with default settings and a WebSock that accepts every connection.
2. Complete the WebSocket upgrade and send a non-final text frame with a 1-byte payload.
3. Send 500,000 masked non-final continuation frames with 1-byte payloads, 3.5 MB in all.
4. Send a Ping. The server answers with a Pong, and BEAM memory has grown by about 82 MB while the message is still far below the 8 MB cap.

## Impact

An unauthenticated client can make one WebSocket connection hold about 150 times `max_fragmented_message_size` in server memory (about 82 MB for 3.5 MB of traffic in the reporter's test). This affects any Bandit server that accepts WebSocket upgrades with default settings, including Phoenix LiveView and Channels apps.

## Workarounds

Lower `websocket_options: [max_fragmented_message_size: ...]` to the largest fragmented message the application needs, for example `65_536`. Memory per connection stays at about 150 times this limit, so a lower limit lowers the ceiling.

summary: AshPostgres ignores attribute multitenancy on the join resource when loading many_to_many and through relationships, returning records related through other tenants' rows
details:
## Summary

Incorrect Authorization vulnerability in ash-project ash_postgres allows a user to load destination records linked to a source record only through another tenant's join rows.

When a `many_to_many` relationship, or a `through` relationship, is loaded with a lateral join (for example with a per-record limit or sort), `AshPostgres.DataLayer` builds the query for the join resource, and for each resource along a `through` path, in `lateral_join_query/3` and `through_step_queries/4` without running that resource's read action, which is where attribute multitenancy is applied. When those resources use `strategy :attribute` multitenancy, rows belonging to other tenants were joined, so the load returned destination records that the caller's tenant is not related to.

This issue affects ash_postgres: from 0.38.0 before 2.15.2.

## Impact

A user of one tenant loading a many_to_many or through relationship receives destination records linked only through another tenant's join rows.

## Configurations

Reachable when the join resource of a `many_to_many` relationship, or a resource along a `through` path, uses attribute multitenancy and holds rows from several tenants, and the relationship is loaded with a lateral join (for example with a limit, offset or sort on the relationship).

summary: Custom cacerts or cacertfile do not restrict trust to the pinned CA in hackney
details:
## Summary

Improper Certificate Validation vulnerability in `hackney_ssl` in benoitc hackney allows an on-path attacker to impersonate a server pinned to a private certificate authority via a certificate chain that ends in a publicly trusted root. hackney adds `{partial_chain, fun hackney_ssl:partial_chain/1}` to every `verify_peer` configuration. The callback returns any certificate in the peer chain whose public key matches a root in the bundled certifi store as the trust anchor, and OTP honours that callback over the configured `cacerts`. `hackney_ssl:merge_ssl_opts/3` kept the callback when the caller replaced the trust store with `cacerts` or `cacertfile` in `ssl_options`, so a connection pinned to a private CA still accepted any chain that carried a publicly trusted root.

The hostname check still applies, so the attacker needs a publicly trusted certificate for the pinned hostname.

This issue affects hackney: from 1.24.0 before 4.9.0.

## Details

**1. Default trust options.** `hackney_ssl:check_hostname_opts/1` builds the `verify_peer` options for every TLS connection: the certifi `cacerts`, a hostname `verify_fun`, and `{partial_chain, fun hackney_ssl:partial_chain/1}`. The callback walks the peer chain and returns `{trusted_ca, Cert}` for the first certificate whose public key matches a root in the bundled certifi store, which lets OTP accept chains that end in a cross-signed root.

**2. Merge keeps the callback.** When the caller passes `ssl_options`, `hackney_ssl:merge_ssl_opts/3` merges them over the defaults with the caller's values winning per key. `cacerts` or `cacertfile` replace the trust store, and a `cacertfile` removes the default `cacerts`, but `partial_chain` has no counterpart in the caller's options and stays.

**3. Validation.** OTP consults `partial_chain` before the configured trust store. A peer chain that carries any publicly trusted root therefore gets that root as its trust anchor, and the pinned `cacerts` are never consulted. Only the hostname `verify_fun` still constrains the attacker.

## Impact

An attacker positioned between the client and a server pinned to a private CA, holding a publicly trusted certificate for the pinned hostname, can impersonate the server and read or modify the traffic the client sends and receives.

## Workarounds

Pass your own `{partial_chain, Fun}` in `ssl_options` alongside `cacerts` or `cacertfile`. A caller-supplied `partial_chain` replaces hackney's in the merge, and a callback that returns `unknown_ca` makes OTP validate against the configured `cacerts` only.

## Configurations

The caller passes `cacerts` or `cacertfile` in `ssl_options` to restrict trust to a private CA, without a `partial_chain` of its own. Connections that use hackney's default certifi trust store are not affected.

summary: Unbounded EIP-7702 authorization list in mpp Tempo fee-payer sponsorship inflates gas cost and sponsors account delegation
details:
## Summary

Improper Validation of Specified Quantity in Input in ZenHive mpp allows an unauthenticated remote client to inflate the fee-payer's gas cost per sponsored payment by a large multiplier and to have the sponsor pay for EIP-7702 account delegations of the client's choosing.

When the server sponsors Tempo payments, `MPP.Methods.Tempo.FeePayerPolicy.measure/3` in `lib/mpp/methods/tempo/fee_payer_policy.ex` bounds the gas fields, the fee budget, the validity window and the access list of the client-signed `0x76` envelope, but never reads its `aa_authorization_list` field. Every signed delegation in that list is charged as intrinsic gas before the payment call runs, so a client attaching delegations from throwaway authority keys makes the sponsor pay for them within the default `gas_limit` ceiling. At the reporter's default of seven entries the sponsored cost rises from about 46,575 gas to about 1,884,087 gas. Because each entry is applied as a persistent set-code delegation, a client can also upgrade its own accounts to delegated code at the sponsor's expense.

This issue affects mpp: from 0.2.0 before 0.16.1.

## Workarounds

Disable Tempo fee sponsorship by leaving `"fee_payer"` at its default of `false` and setting no `fee_payer_url`, so the client pays its own gas. Where sponsorship must stay enabled, lower the `max_gas` override in `fee_payer_policy` to just above what a legitimate sponsored payment needs (a TIP-20 transfer is roughly 50,000 gas), so an envelope padded with delegations either fails the policy or runs out of gas at a bounded cost. This bounds the inflation without closing it.

## Configurations

Only deployments that enable Tempo server-side fee sponsorship are affected, through `"fee_payer" => true` in `method_config` with either local co-signing (`fee_payer_private_key`) or hosted sponsorship (`fee_payer_url`). Sponsorship is disabled by default.

summary: Unbounded key authorization in mpp Tempo fee-payer sponsorship inflates gas cost and sponsors access-key provisioning
details:
## Summary

Improper Validation of Specified Quantity in Input in ZenHive mpp allows an unauthenticated remote client to inflate the fee-payer's gas cost per sponsored payment by a large multiplier and to have the sponsor pay for provisioning an access key on the client's own account.

When the server sponsors Tempo payments, `MPP.Methods.Tempo.FeePayerPolicy.measure/3` in `lib/mpp/methods/tempo/fee_payer_policy.ex` bounds the gas fields, the fee budget, the validity window and the access list of the client-signed `0x76` envelope, but does not check whether the envelope carries the optional `key_authorization` field. A client can attach a fully signed key authorization, provisioning a new access key with token spending limits on its own account, alongside the normal payment call. The key and each limit entry are persistent storage writes billed as intrinsic gas to the sponsor, bounded only by the `gas_limit` ceiling. At the reporter's default of one key with three token limits the sponsored cost rises from about 46,587 gas to about 1,808,700 gas, and the client keeps a valid access key it paid nothing for.

This issue affects mpp: from 0.2.0 before 0.16.1.

## Workarounds

Disable Tempo fee sponsorship by leaving `"fee_payer"` at its default of `false` and setting no `fee_payer_url`, so the client pays its own gas. Where sponsorship must stay enabled, lower the `max_gas` override in `fee_payer_policy` to just above what a legitimate sponsored payment needs (a TIP-20 transfer is roughly 50,000 gas), so an envelope carrying a key authorization either fails the policy or runs out of gas at a bounded cost. This bounds the inflation without closing it.

## Configurations

Only deployments that enable Tempo server-side fee sponsorship are affected, through `"fee_payer" => true` in `method_config` with either local co-signing (`fee_payer_private_key`) or hosted sponsorship (`fee_payer_url`). Sponsorship is disabled by default.

summary: Ash.Filter.Runtime materializes a combinatorial cross-product over to-many relationships, exhausting memory
details:
## Summary

Uncontrolled Resource Consumption vulnerability in ash-project ash lets an attacker exhaust node memory by matching a filter that spans multiple to-many relationships in memory.

`Ash.Filter.Runtime` matches a filter against an in-memory record by first expanding the record into combinations of its related rows. `flatten_relationships/2` (`lib/ash/filter/runtime.ex`) eagerly built the full Cartesian product across the filter's to-many relationship paths, so a record with K to-many relationships of M rows each materialized on the order of M^K scenarios before any predicate was checked. A filter or dataset that reaches several sizeable to-many relationships therefore allocates memory combinatorially and can exhaust the node. The fix streams the expansion lazily and short-circuits on the first matching scenario, bounding the work.

This issue affects ash: from 1.29.0-rc0 before 3.32.2.

summary: Unbounded response body buffering and decompression in hackney
details:
## Summary

Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling vulnerability in `hackney_conn` in benoitc hackney allows a malicious HTTP server to exhaust client memory via an oversized or highly compressed response body. `hackney:request/5` and `hackney:body/1` return the whole response body, and nothing bounds how much the connection process buffers. Any server the client requests can trigger it.

`hackney_conn:read_full_body/2` and the HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 accumulators append every chunk until the body ends. With `{auto_decompress, true}` the buffered body is then inflated in one step with `zlib:gunzip/1` or `zlib:inflate/2`, which return the whole output at once.

This issue affects hackney: from 2.0.0-beta.1 before 4.9.0.

## Details

**1. Unbounded accumulation.** `hackney:request/5` with a body, and `hackney:body/1` after `start_response/1`, read the response in `src/hackney_conn.erl` through `read_full_body/2`, which appends each chunk to a binary accumulator until the body ends. The HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 synchronous paths accumulate stream data the same way. No option caps the size.

**2. One-step decompression.** With `{auto_decompress, true}` hackney sends `Accept-Encoding: gzip, deflate`. Once the body is complete, `maybe_decompress_body/2` dispatches on `Content-Encoding` to `decompress_gzip/1` (`zlib:gunzip/1`) or `decompress_deflate/1` (`zlib:inflate/2`). Both return the whole output at once, so the inflated size is bounded only by the compression ratio. The report measured a 1 MB gzip body inflating to 1 GB on hackney 4.8.4.

## Proof of concept

1. Build a gzip stream whose inflated size is 1 GB from a reused 64 KB chunk of zero bytes (deflate with window bits 31, best compression). The stream is about 1 MB on the wire.
2. Start a TCP listener on loopback that accepts one connection, reads the request, and answers `HTTP/1.1 200 OK` with `Content-Encoding: gzip`, a `Content-Length` matching the stream, `Connection: close`, and the stream as body.
3. From a node running a vulnerable hackney, call `hackney:request(get, Url, [], <<>>, [{auto_decompress, true}, with_body])` against that listener.
4. Observe the returned body of 1,048,576,000 bytes and the VM memory growing by about 1.8 GB for a 1,019,197 byte response. A larger stream, or an endless body without `auto_decompress`, drives the node out of memory.

## Impact

A server the client requests can make the client allocate memory proportional to the body it sends, or to its decompressed size, until the node runs out of memory.

## Workarounds

Leave `auto_decompress` disabled (the default). Without it `hackney_conn:maybe_decompress_body/2` never inflates the body, which closes the amplification half. The uncapped raw body read has no workaround.

summary: Ash string length constraints count graphemes, so a combining-mark string of any size passes max_length
details:
## Summary

Improper Validation of Specified Quantity in Input vulnerability in ash-project ash allows an attacker to store a value of arbitrary size in an attribute whose length constraint should bound it.

Ash measures string length with Elixir's `String.length/1`, which counts Unicode graphemes, in the `max_length` and `min_length` constraints of `Ash.Type.String` (`apply_constraints/2` in `lib/ash/type/string.ex`), in `Ash.Resource.Validation.StringLength`, and in the `string_length` expression function. A grapheme carries an unbounded number of combining marks, so a base character followed by a million combining acute accents is one grapheme and megabytes of data, and satisfies `max_length: 2`. Where the data layer imposes no independent limit (ETS, Mnesia, or a Postgres `text` column) the whole value is persisted, so an attacker can write an entire request body into an attribute declared with a small maximum and grow storage without bound.

The counting unit also disagrees with the storage layer, which counts codepoints rather than graphemes, so a value accepted by the constraint can still be rejected or truncated by the column. A Postgres `varchar(n)` column bounds the value itself and is not exposed.

This issue affects ash: from 0.10.0 before 3.33.0.

## Configurations

A resource attribute must carry a `max_length` constraint (or an equivalent `string_length` validation) fed from client input, and the data layer must impose no independent size limit of its own. The ETS and Mnesia data layers and Postgres `text` columns store the value in full; a Postgres `varchar(n)` column bounds it independently and is not exposed.

summary: Ash.Type.CiString validates length and match constraints before case folding, allowing constraint bypass
details:
## Summary

Incorrect Behavior Order: Validate Before Canonicalize vulnerability in ash-project ash lets an attacker store a case-insensitive string value that violates its length or match constraints.

`Ash.Type.CiString.apply_constraints/2` (`lib/ash/type/ci_string.ex`) validated the `max_length`, `min_length`, and `match` constraints against the value as submitted, while the type case-folds the string (per its `casing`) for storage and comparison. Because validation ran before folding, an attacker can submit a value whose folded form breaks a constraint but whose original form passes: for example, against a match pattern requiring uppercase, an uppercase value that is stored lowercased persists a value the pattern rejects. The fix case-folds the value at the start of `apply_constraints/2`, so the constraints are checked against the form that is actually stored.

This issue affects ash: from 1.29.0-rc0 before 3.32.2.

summary: Ash.Type.UUIDv7 accepts non-v7 UUIDs that then fail to load, causing persistent denial of service
details:
## Summary

Improper Input Validation vulnerability in ash-project ash allows an attacker to persistently deny reads of a record by storing a non-version-7 UUID in an `Ash.Type.UUIDv7` attribute.

`Ash.Type.UUIDv7.cast_input/2` accepts any well-formed UUID string, including non-version-7 UUIDs, and stores it as a 16-byte binary. On read, `cast_stored/2` (`lib/ash/type/uuid_v7.ex`) routes the stored binary back through `cast_input/2`, which since an input-validation tightening in v3.6.3 matches only version-7 (and optionally version-4) 16-byte binaries and otherwise expects a 36-character string. A stored non-v7 16-byte binary matches neither clause and returns `:error`, so every later read of that record fails. An attacker able to set such an attribute poisons the row permanently. The fix decodes any 16-byte stored binary directly in `cast_stored/2`.

This issue affects ash: from 3.6.3 before 3.32.2.

summary: Ash.update_many/4 atomic path skips resource policy authorization, allowing updates to forbidden records
details:
## Summary

Missing Authorization vulnerability in ash-project ash allows an actor to update records forbidden by resource policies through the atomic path of `Ash.update_many/4`.

`Ash.update_many/4` runs as a single atomic statement (a data-layer `update_many`, for example a SQL MERGE) whenever an atomic strategy is used and the data layer supports it. `Ash.Actions.Update.UpdateMany` (`lib/ash/actions/update/update_many.ex`) took that path even under `authorize?: true` without applying the resource's policies, so the statement updated every row matched by primary key regardless of the policy filter that authorization would impose. An actor could therefore update records the policies forbid, such as rows belonging to another actor or tenant. The fix restricts the atomic path to data layers supporting changeset filters when authorizing, authorizes each changeset, and merges the resulting policy filter into each changeset so the statement only touches authorized rows.

This issue affects ash: from 3.29.0 before 3.32.2.

summary: Non-finite Infinity/NaN decimal values bypass bounds constraints in Ash.Type.Decimal
details:
## Summary

Improper Validation of Specified Quantity in Input vulnerability in ash-project ash allows an attacker to submit a non-finite decimal value that bypasses numeric bounds constraints or fails later operations on the value.

`Ash.Type.Decimal` cast input through Ecto's decimal cast in `cast_input/2` and `cast_stored/2` (`lib/ash/type/decimal.ex`) without checking that the resulting value is finite. Elixir's `Decimal` represents `Infinity` and `NaN` as valid structs, so a value such as `"Infinity"` or `"NaN"` passed casting and was persisted. Because `NaN` compares as false against every bound, `min` and `max` constraints do not reject it, and the stored special value later raises when used in `Decimal` arithmetic or is refused by the data layer, failing subsequent requests. The fix rejects any non-finite `Decimal` during casting.

This issue affects ash: from 1.28.0 before 3.32.2.

summary: Quadratic chunk-size parsing in Mint.HTTP1.Parse allows CPU-exhaustion DoS
details:
## Summary

Inefficient Algorithmic Complexity vulnerability in elixir-mint mint allows a remote HTTP server to exhaust CPU on the client host and cause a denial of service.

`parse_hex_prefix/2` in `lib/mint/http1/parse.ex` folds each hex digit of a chunked response's chunk-size field into an arbitrary-precision accumulator with `acc * 16 + digit` and imposes no limit on the digit count. Because the accumulator grows without bound, the multiplication is not constant time and one pass over `N` digits costs O(N squared). `handle_data/2` prepends `conn.buffer` and re-parses from the start on every socket message, so a server that dribbles the digits out in small packets makes the client pay that cost repeatedly. A run of roughly 512,000 hex digits costs over ten seconds of CPU in a single pass, measured on stock defaults. The parser reaches this state after a valid status line and a complete, valid header section, so an intermediary inspecting only headers sees an ordinary 200 response.

This issue affects mint: from 1.9.3 before 1.10.0.

summary: AshPhoenix FilterForm allows filtering across non-public relationships, disclosing private related data
details:
## Summary

Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key vulnerability in ash-project ash_phoenix lets an attacker who controls filter form parameters filter across relationships the resource author marked non-public, turning the returned rows into a boolean oracle over private related data.

`AshPhoenix.FilterForm` resolved every relationship hop in the user-supplied `path` with `Ash.Resource.Info.related/2`, which traverses private relationships, and only checked the terminal field for publicity. `parse_path_and_field/2` also rewrote a `field` naming a relationship into an extra path segment, so `field=some_private_rel` was accepted too. Both `path` and `field` come straight from form params, and the resulting ref went to `Ash.Query.do_filter/2` without the public-only enforcement of `Ash.Filter.parse_input/2`. The fix resolves each hop with `Ash.Resource.Info.public_relationship/2`, rejecting the first non-public hop, and requires the terminal field to be public.

This issue affects ash_phoenix: from 0.6.0-rc.1 before 2.3.25.

## Configurations

The resource exposes an `AshPhoenix.FilterForm` whose params the attacker controls, and has a non-public relationship to data that should not be filterable.

summary: AshPhoenix Form.Auto leaks submitted params in an unknown _union_type error message
details:
## Summary

Generation of Error Message Containing Sensitive Information vulnerability in ash-project ash_phoenix writes the entire raw submitted param map into an exception message, so secrets submitted alongside a union form field leak into logs, crash reports and the dev error page.

When `AshPhoenix.Form.Auto` builds a union sub-form and the submitted `_union_type` does not match a configured type, both raise sites built the message with `inspect(params, pretty: true)`, embedding the full untrusted param map, and also inspected the internal union `constraints[:types]`. Because the message is constructed by the library rather than Phoenix's parameter logger, `config :phoenix, :filter_parameters` never redacts it. An attacker controls both the trigger and the contents: submitting `%{"_union_type" => "nope", "password" => "..."}` puts the password verbatim in the raised message. The fix reports only the offending `_union_type` and the valid type names, dropping the param and constraints dumps.

This issue affects ash_phoenix: from 1.2.17 before 2.3.25.

## Configurations

The application renders an `AshPhoenix.Form` with a union field, and submitted params (which may carry secrets) reach logs, crash reports or the error page.

summary: AshPhoenix get_subdomain maps a crafted or differently-cased Host header to an arbitrary tenant
details:
## Summary

Permissive Regular Expression vulnerability in ash-project ash_phoenix lets a remote client select the tenant an Ash application uses, or degrade the request, by sending a crafted `Host` header.

`AshPhoenix.Helpers.get_subdomain/2` stripped the root domain with `String.replace(host, ~r/.?#{root_host}/, "")`. The root host was interpolated raw, so each `.` became a wildcard and any metacharacter a pattern, and the replace was global and unanchored, so a match was removed from anywhere in the string. With `root_host` `example.com`, `Host: foo.exampleXcom.attacker.net` returned the tenant `foo.attacker.net`. A metacharacter-bearing or `nil` root host degraded the pattern or raised on every request. The comparison was also case-sensitive, so `TENANT.EXAMPLE.COM` and `EXAMPLE.COM` slipped past the root-host allowlist. `conn.host` comes from the client `Host` header. The fix matches the root host case-insensitively and only as an exact trailing suffix.

This issue affects ash_phoenix: from 2.1.26 before 2.3.25.

## Configurations

The application uses subdomain-based multitenancy via `AshPhoenix.Helpers.get_subdomain/2` (for example through `AshPhoenix.LiveView.SubdomainHook`) to select the tenant from the request host.

summary: Declared argument constraints not enforced on AshTypescript typed controller routes
details:
## Summary
