Improper Input Validation vulnerability in ash-project ash_typescript allows a remote attacker to submit argument values outside a declared allowlist or bound on typed-controller routes.

`AshTypescript.TypedController.RequestHandler` in `lib/ash_typescript/typed_controller/request_handler.ex` calls `Ash.Type.cast_input/3` and treats an `{:ok, cast}` result as fully validated. In Ash these are separate steps: `cast_input/3` only coerces the term, while every constraint declared on the argument is applied by `Ash.Type.apply_constraints/3`, which this path never calls. Constraints such as `one_of`, `max_length`, `min` and `max`, and `match` are therefore inert, so a value outside a declared allowlist is accepted and passed to the route handler. Codegen renders the same constraints into the generated TypeScript types, so an allowlist appears enforced to a TypeScript caller while any other HTTP client ignores it. Empty-string to `nil` normalization also lives in `apply_constraints`, so the `allow_nil?: false` check accepts `""` for a required argument.

Where a constraint gates a role, a status, or a sort direction, this becomes a privilege or state-machine bypass.

This issue affects ash_typescript: from 0.15.0 before 0.18.0.

## Configurations

The application exposes an AshTypescript typed controller over HTTP with at least one route argument carrying a `constraints` declaration that gates application behaviour.

summary: Unbounded HTTP/1 status-line and chunk-extension buffering in Mint causes memory-exhaustion DoS
details:
## Summary

Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling vulnerability in elixir-mint mint allows a remote HTTP server to exhaust memory on the client host and cause a denial of service.

Two HTTP/1 response-parser states accumulate server data without any cap. In `lib/mint/http1.ex`, `decode_status_line/4` stores the unconsumed data in `conn.buffer` when the status line is incomplete, and `decode_body/5` does the same for an unterminated chunk-extension line. Both wait for a CRLF the server never has to send, and `conn.buffer` is prepended to every subsequent socket message. The `:max_header_list_size` budget is wired only into `decode_headers/5` and `decode_trailer_headers/4`, so neither of these states is covered by it. A malicious server, or one reached through an attacker-controlled redirect or a fetched URL, streams bytes indefinitely until the BEAM node is killed by the operating system out-of-memory handler. The chunk-extension variant is reached after a valid status line and a complete, valid header section, so an intermediary inspecting only headers sees an ordinary 200 response.

This issue affects mint: from 0.1.0 before 1.10.0.

summary: Terminal escape sequence injection in mix usage_rules.search_docs via package documentation metadata
details:
## Summary

Improper Neutralization of Escape, Meta, or Control Sequences vulnerability in ash-project usage_rules allows a malicious package publisher to inject terminal control sequences into the output of `mix usage_rules.search_docs`.

`mix usage_rules.search_docs` searches Hex documentation through `search.hexdocs.pm`, which indexes the documentation of every published package, and prints the matching results (title, package, type, doc reference, and highlighted snippets) to the terminal. The formatter in `Mix.Tasks.UsageRules.SearchDocs` interpolated those publisher-controlled fields verbatim, neutralizing no terminal control characters; the only transform it applied adds escape sequences rather than removing them. A malicious package can embed ANSI terminal escape sequences (cursor movement, line erase, carriage returns, OSC 52 clipboard writes) in its indexed documentation, so when a developer runs a search that surfaces those docs the sequences reach the terminal unchanged — forging the displayed hexdocs URL or a suggested command, hiding text, or writing to the clipboard. No authentication or privileged position is required; only publishing a package.

This issue affects usage_rules: from 0.1.18 before 1.2.8.

## Configurations

Reachable only when a developer runs `mix usage_rules.search_docs` in a terminal emulator that interprets ANSI escape sequences and the results include documentation from an attacker-published package (for example a broad `--everywhere` search).

summary: Route handler return value echoed into AshTypescript error response
details:
## Summary

Generation of Error Message Containing Sensitive Information vulnerability in ash-project ash_typescript allows an unauthenticated attacker to read internal application data from an HTTP 500 response body.

When a typed-controller route handler returns anything other than a `%Plug.Conn{}`, `dispatch/3` in `lib/ash_typescript/typed_controller/request_handler.ex` passes the value to `unexpected_return/2`, which interpolates `inspect(value, limit: 50)` directly into the response message. The `limit` option bounds elements per collection rather than the term as a whole, so a handler falling through with a term such as `{:error, %User{}}` or a changeset serialises its full field set, including hashed passwords, tokens, and tenant identifiers, into the JSON error returned to the caller.

This contradicts the module's own posture elsewhere: the `rescue` clause gates `Exception.message/1` behind `AshTypescript.typed_controller_show_raised_errors?/0` and otherwise returns a generic message, while this path is ungated and always echoes.

This issue affects ash_typescript: from 0.15.0 before 0.18.0.

## Configurations

The application exposes an AshTypescript typed controller over HTTP with a route handler that can return a non-`Plug.Conn` term carrying sensitive data.

summary: AshAdmin LiveView events intern atoms from client input, exhausting the atom table (node DoS)
details:
## Summary

Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling vulnerability in ash-project ash_admin lets any client that can reach the admin LiveView exhaust the BEAM atom table and crash the entire node.

Two LiveView event handlers interned atoms from unvalidated client input: `AshAdmin.PageLive`'s `set_actor` built modules from the `resource`/`domain` payload with `Module.concat/1`, and `AshAdmin.Components.Resource.Show`'s `calculate` converted every submitted form key with `String.to_atom/1`. Atoms are never garbage collected and the table is capped, so flooding either event with random names mints a new atom per request until the VM aborts, taking down every application on the node. The fix resolves the submitted `resource`/`domain` against the known shown resources and maps calculation keys to declared arguments, so no client-supplied string is interned.

This issue affects ash_admin: from 0.1.0 before 1.3.1.

summary: Terminal escape sequence injection in the mix igniter.install confirmation prompt via package metadata
details:
## Summary

Improper Neutralization of Escape, Meta, or Control Sequences vulnerability in ash-project igniter allows a malicious package publisher to forge the `mix igniter.install` confirmation prompt.

`mix igniter.install` prints a confirmation panel (an anti-typosquatting safeguard) listing a package's hex metadata before adding it. The panel builder in `Igniter.Project.Deps` wrote publisher-controlled fields (`meta.description`, owner usernames, requirement names, version) to the terminal with only newlines stripped. A malicious or typosquatted package can embed ANSI terminal escape sequences (cursor movement, line erase, carriage returns) in its metadata to overwrite the panel, forging trusted author names and download counts while concealing the real ones, so a developer relying on the panel to vet the package is deceived into approving a malicious dependency.

This issue affects igniter: from 0.8.1 before 0.8.4.

## Configurations

Reachable only when a developer runs `mix igniter.install` against an untrusted or misspelled package name in a terminal emulator that interprets ANSI escape sequences.

summary: Actor record with password digest stored in AshAuthentication audit log entries
details:
## Summary

Insertion of Sensitive Information into Log File vulnerability in team-alembic AshAuthentication allows disclosure of user password digests to readers of the audit store.

The `audit_log` add-on builds each entry's `extra_data` in `AshAuthentication.AddOn.AuditLog.Auditor.build_extra_data/4`, which takes `:actor` from the action callback context verbatim. Any audited action invoked with `actor:` set to a user record therefore deposits that record, including its `hashed_password` attribute, into the audit entry. The same module already collapses the audited identity to an opaque string via `AshAuthentication.user_to_subject/1` and filters `params` against the strategy's configured allow-list, so the actor is the only stored value that reaches the audit store unfiltered. Marking the attribute `sensitive?: true` does not help, because that redacts `inspect/1` output rather than JSON encoding or raw-term storage.

There is no attacker-controlled trigger and no network disclosure path: entries accumulate from ordinary authenticated activity, and an attacker's own requests deposit only their own digest. Exploitation requires independent read access to the audit store, such as database credentials, an audit role, a backup, or a log shipper, at which point the digests support offline password attack against every active account. Whether the material persists depends on the data layer, since raw-term stores keep it verbatim while a SQL store raises `Protocol.UndefinedError` and drops the entry unless the user resource derives `Jason.Encoder`.

This issue affects ash_authentication: from 4.12.0 before 4.15.0 and from 5.0.0-rc.0 before 5.0.0-rc.2.

summary: Ash.Vector wraps the 16-bit dimension header for vectors over 65,535 elements, corrupting data and crashing reads
details:
## Summary

Integer Overflow or Wraparound vulnerability in ash-project ash lets an attacker corrupt a stored vector and crash later reads of it by submitting a vector with more than 65,535 elements.

`Ash.Vector.new/1` (`lib/ash/vector.ex`) encodes a vector as `<<dim::unsigned-16, 0::unsigned-16>>` followed by the element floats, packing the element count into a 16-bit field without checking its range. A list of more than 65,535 elements wraps the dimension modulo 65,536, so the encoded header records a dimension that disagrees with the number of stored floats. `from_binary/1` later reads `binary-size(dim)-unit(32)` from the wrapped header, so every read of the corrupted value misparses and raises, denying access to the affected record. The fix rejects any vector whose dimension exceeds 65,535.

This issue affects ash: from 2.14.13 before 3.32.2.

summary: Ash.Type.Union with :map_with_tag does not force the tag on dump, enabling tag confusion
details:
## Summary

Improper Validation of Specified Type of Input vulnerability in ash-project ash lets an attacker confuse the stored type tag of an `Ash.Type.Union` value that uses `storage: :map_with_tag`, bypassing that member's validation and any tag-based authorization.

For a union with `storage: :map_with_tag`, each member is identified in storage by a configured `tag` and `tag_value`. `Ash.Type.Union.dump_to_native/2` (`lib/ash/type/union.ex`) did not force the configured tag when writing the value, so a tag carried in the submitted value was persisted verbatim. An attacker can therefore store a value whose data belongs to one member but whose tag names a different member. On read the value is re-selected by its tag and treated as the incompatible member (a type confusion), bypassing the real member's constraints and any logic or policy that branches on the union tag. The fix drops any incoming tag and forces the configured tag value on dump.

This issue affects ash: from 2.14.18 before 3.32.2.

summary: Ash.Actions.Read.AsyncLimiter busy-spins a scheduler while awaiting slow async reads
details:
## Summary

Uncontrolled Resource Consumption vulnerability in ash-project ash lets a slow asynchronous read spin a scheduler thread at full CPU while the framework waits for it.

`Ash.Actions.Read.AsyncLimiter.await_at_least_one/1` (`lib/ash/actions/read/async_limiter.ex`) waited for concurrent async read tasks by polling each with `Task.yield(task, 0)` in a tight loop rather than blocking. While every outstanding task is still running (a slow related-data load or calculation), the loop returns immediately and repeats, busy-spinning and holding a BEAM scheduler at full CPU for the whole duration of the slow read; concurrent slow reads tie up further schedulers. The fix waits with `Task.yield_many` (a non-blocking sweep followed by a blocking wait with `timeout: :infinity`), so the process sleeps until a task completes instead of spinning.

This issue affects ash: from 2.19.0 before 3.32.2.

summary: Authorization-redacted field values disclosed through AshTypescript result normalization
details:
## Summary

Incorrect Authorization vulnerability in ash-project ash_typescript allows an unauthorized RPC caller to read attribute values that Ash field policies denied.

When a field policy denies an attribute, Ash substitutes `%Ash.ForbiddenField{}`, which retains the real value in `original_value` because embedded resources must remain writable, and hides it from `Inspect` rather than removing it. `AshTypescript.Rpc.ResultProcessor` strips these markers to `nil` on its template-driven paths, but `normalize_primitive/1` in `lib/ash_typescript/rpc/result_processor.ex` had no such clause, so a marker fell through to the generic struct branch which calls `Map.from_struct/1` and serializes every key, `original_value` included. The denied value is returned to the caller inside the marker that represents its own denial.

The simplest trigger is an action returning an embedded resource as a map, which routes through `normalize_resource_struct/2` with an empty template. `normalize_value_for_json/1` is a public, unguarded entry point to the same path.

This issue affects ash_typescript: from 0.11.0 before 0.18.0.

## Configurations

The application exposes an AshTypescript RPC endpoint over HTTP and relies on Ash field policies to hide attributes on embedded resources that an action returns as a map.

summary: Boruta dynamic client registration allows creation of over-privileged OAuth clients
details:
## Summary

Improper Isolation or Compartmentalization vulnerability in malach-it boruta (`Boruta.Openid` module) allows attackers to register OpenID Connect clients with administrative privileges through the dynamic client registration entry point. `Boruta.Openid.register_client/3` forwards caller-supplied registration parameters to the administrative client creation path without a public/admin field-level allowlist, so an unauthenticated registrant can set security-sensitive attributes including supported grant types, authorized scopes, PKCE enforcement, public refresh and revocation behavior, token lifetimes, and signing settings. The library does not distinguish between metadata a public registrant is allowed to set and administrative controls that should require operator approval.

This vulnerability is associated with program files `lib/boruta/openid.ex` and program routines `Boruta.Openid.register_client/3`, `Boruta.Openid.parse_registration_params/2`.

This issue affects boruta: from 2.3.0 before 2.3.7 and from 3.0.0-beta.1 onward.

## Workarounds

Disable the dynamic client registration route or restrict it to authenticated administrators. If dynamic registration must remain available to untrusted callers, do not forward the request parameters to `Boruta.Openid.register_client/3` directly. Instead, construct a new parameter map in the host application that contains only the standards-defined public metadata (such as redirect URIs, client name, logo, and contacts) and overwrite every administrative attribute (supported grant types, authorized scopes, PKCE flag, public refresh and revocation flags, token lifetimes, signing settings, token endpoint authentication method) with values from a fixed least-privilege server-side profile before calling the function.

## Configurations

A deployment is vulnerable when the host application exposes `Boruta.Openid.register_client/3` on a network endpoint without requiring a trusted initial access token and without a strict server-side allowlist that prevents caller-supplied administrative attributes from reaching the underlying changeset. The standard controller generator does not install a dynamic client registration route, so deployments that never call `Boruta.Openid.register_client/3` from a public endpoint are not exploitable.

summary: AshLua read operation aggregate bypasses the exposed-field allow-list, exposing private attributes
details:
## Summary

Improper Protection of Alternate Path vulnerability in ash-project ash_lua allows a user-supplied Lua script to read attributes that are not on the exposed-field allow-list.

AshLua exposes Ash resources to Lua scripts, gated by a manifest declaring which fields are exposed. The `read` action's `operation` aggregate path in `AshLua.Runtime` took the field name straight from the Lua call and resolved it with only `String.to_existing_atom` and `Ash.Query.Aggregate.new!`, neither of which consults the exposed-field allow-list the normal `fields` path enforces. A script can therefore read the value of any attribute of any record the actor may read, including private `sensitive?: true` columns, via `resource.read({ operation = {"list", "hashed_password"} })`; `min` and `max` give a value oracle. Anyone able to submit or influence a Lua script can reach this.

This issue affects ash_lua: from 0.1.0 before 0.2.1.

## Configurations

Reachable only when an application exposes AshLua scripting (the `AshLua.Resource` / `AshLua.Domain` extensions) to callers who can submit or influence Lua scripts, and the exposed resource has attributes that are not on the exposed-field surface.

summary: html_sanitize_ex HTML5 scrubber keeps attacker-supplied form-association attributes, allowing form hijacking
details:
## Summary

URL Redirection to Untrusted Site ('Open Redirect') vulnerability in the HTML5 scrubber in rrrene html_sanitize_ex allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to retarget a form already on the rendering page and receive whatever the victim submits, including credentials, via the `form` and `formaction` attributes on an `<input>` element in sanitized HTML. HTML's `form` attribute associates an input with any form on the page by its `id` even when the input sits outside that form, and `formaction` on a submit control overrides the owning form's `action`. Neither attribute receives a scheme check, so an absolute cross-origin URL survives sanitizing.

No script executes. The scrubber allows neither `form` nor `button`, so the attacker cannot introduce a form of their own and the rendering page must already contain a form carrying an `id`.

This issue affects html_sanitize_ex: from 0.3.1 before 1.4.5 and from 1.5.0-rc.0 before 1.5.3.

## Workarounds

Sanitize with `basic_html/1`, `markdown_html/1` or `strip_tags/1`, none of which allow `input`, or define a custom scrubber that omits it.

Omitting the `id` attribute from the page's own forms, or giving them values an attacker cannot predict, removes the anchor the injected `form` attribute needs.

## Configurations

Only `HtmlSanitizeEx.html5/1`, and custom scrubbers declared with `use HtmlSanitizeEx, extend: :html5`, allow the `input` element, and the sanitized output must be rendered to other users.

The rendering page must also contain a form with an `id`, since that `id` is what the injected `form` attribute binds to.

summary: ECDSA signature length is not validated in jose, allowing signature malleability
details:
## Summary

The `jose` library accepts ECDSA (ES256, ES256K, ES384, and ES512) JWS signatures of a non-canonical length. When verifying an ECDSA signature, `jose_jwk_kty_ec:verify/4` in `src/jwk/jose_jwk_kty_ec.erl` splits the raw signature in half by its actual byte length (`split_binary(Signature, byte_size(Signature) div 2)`) instead of enforcing the fixed length required by RFC 7518 §3.4, and then decodes each half with `crypto:bytes_to_integer/1`, which ignores leading zero bytes.

As a result, an attacker who holds one valid token can prepend leading zero bytes to each of the R and S halves to produce longer signatures that still split evenly and decode to the same `(r, s)` pair, so many distinct signature byte strings all verify against the same key (signature malleability). This does not allow forging new payloads or impersonating a signer, because the underlying `(r, s)` values are unchanged. It does defeat any security control that assumes a valid token or its signature is unique, such as token-revocation-by-hash, replay or idempotency caches, and deduplication logic.

This issue affects jose: from 1.0.0 before 1.11.13.

summary: Bleichenbacher padding oracle in RSAES-PKCS1-v1_5 decryption in jose
details:
## Summary

The pure-Erlang RSAES-PKCS1-v1_5 decryption in the `jose_jwa_pkcs1` module is a Bleichenbacher padding oracle. `eme_pkcs1_decode/2` returns the recovered message when a decrypted block has valid `PKCS#1` v1.5 padding (a leading `0x00 0x02`, a padding string of at least eight non-zero bytes, and a `0x00` separator) and returns a distinct error result otherwise, and `rsaes_pkcs1_decrypt/2` additionally returns `{error, {badsize, _}}` when the length check fails. The implementation applies no implicit-rejection countermeasure (RFC 8017 §7.2.2): it does not substitute a deterministic pseudo-random plaintext on a padding failure, so a one-bit padding-conformance signal leaks to the caller. Because the underlying modular exponentiation in `dp/2` is a raw, non-blinded `crypto:mod_pow/3`, the padding check also stays distinguishable by timing even when an application normalizes every failure to a single error value.

An unauthenticated attacker who knows only the public RSA key and can submit ciphertexts to a decryption endpoint that unwraps RSA1_5 JWE keys (or otherwise calls `decrypt_private/3` with `rsa_pkcs1_padding`) can use this oracle to recover the plaintext of intercepted ciphertexts, such as content-encryption keys and thus the protected message, or to forge signatures, through roughly 10^4 to 10^6 adaptive chosen-ciphertext queries.

This issue affects jose: from 1.3.0 before 1.11.13.

## Configurations

The vulnerable code path is only reached when jose performs RSAES-PKCS1-v1_5 decryption with its pure-Erlang fallback (the `jose_jwa_pkcs1` module) instead of the native OTP `public_key` implementation. This requires the crypto_fallback option to be enabled (`application:set_env(jose, crypto_fallback, true)`, or `JOSE.crypto_fallback(true)` in Elixir) and the OTP runtime not to provide native RSA1_5 decryption. When native OTP RSA support is selected, decryption does not go through `jose_jwa_pkcs1`.

summary: Timing side-channel in pure-Erlang X25519 scalar multiplication leaks the private key in jose
details:
## Summary

Observable Timing Discrepancy vulnerability in potatosalad jose allows recovery of a long-term X25519 private key through a timing side channel in the pure-Erlang Curve25519 fallback.

The pure-Erlang X25519 implementation performs scalar multiplication over the secret private key using a recursive Montgomery ladder (`jose_jwa_x25519:curve25519/2`) whose clauses branch on individual bits of the clamped private scalar, and whose per-step operations (`jose_jwa_x25519:montgomery_add/3` and `jose_jwa_x25519:montgomery_double/1`) and field inversion are built from value-dependent Erlang bignum arithmetic (multiplication, remainder, and modular exponentiation). Although the ladder is operation-count balanced and fixed at 254 steps, the concrete integer values processed at each step, and therefore the running time, depend on the secret scalar. The execution time of the public entry points `jose_jwa_x25519:scalarmult/2`, `jose_jwa_x25519:x25519/2`, `jose_jwa_x25519:x25519_base/1`, and `jose_jwa_x25519:sk_to_pk/1` is thus a function of the private key.

This path is reachable from the public API, most notably when a service decrypts attacker-supplied ECDH-ES (JWE) messages with a long-term X25519 key (for example through `JOSE.JWK.box_decrypt_ecdh_es/2`, which reaches `jose_jwa_curve25519:x25519_shared_secret/2` and the ladder). An attacker who can submit ciphertexts and measure decryption timing can, in principle, recover the private key bit by bit, defeating the resistance X25519 was designed to provide. Recovery of the key compromises the confidentiality and authenticity of all data protected by it.

This issue affects jose: from 1.10.0 before 1.11.13.

## Workarounds

Use a constant-time native X25519 implementation for private-key operations: install the libsodium or libdecaf NIF, or run on an OTP release whose `crypto` application provides `x25519`, and do not force the pure-Erlang Curve25519 fallback (`JOSE.crypto_fallback(true)` or `JOSE.curve25519_module(:jose_jwa_curve25519)`) for long-lived keys.

## Configurations

The vulnerability is only exploitable when X25519 private-key operations run through the pure-Erlang Curve25519 fallback, for example when the crypto fallback is enabled (`JOSE.crypto_fallback(true)` or `JOSE.curve25519_module(:jose_jwa_curve25519)`) or when no constant-time native X25519 implementation (a libsodium or libdecaf NIF, or the OTP `crypto` application providing `x25519`) is available. Deployments that use a constant-time native X25519 are not affected.

summary: erlang-jose RSA JWK parsing attempts to factor an attacker-controlled modulus, enabling CPU-exhaustion denial of service
details:
## Summary

Inefficient Algorithmic Complexity in erlang-jose allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to cause a CPU-exhaustion denial of service by submitting a crafted RSA JSON Web Key.

When an application parses an untrusted JWK through the public `jose_jwk:from_binary/1` or `jose_jwk:from_map/1` API (or the Elixir wrappers `JOSE.JWK.from_binary/1` and `JOSE.JWK.from_map/1`), an RSA private key that supplies `d`, `e`, and `n` but omits all Chinese Remainder Theorem parameters (`p`, `q`, `dp`, `dq`, `qi`) is routed into `convert_sfm_to_crt/1`, which tries to recover the missing primes by factoring the modulus. The three integers are read straight from the base64url input and are never validated as a real RSA key. When the modulus cannot be split into two factors (for example, when it is itself prime), the search loop `convert_sfm_to_crt_find_p/6` performs a modular exponentiation over the attacker-sized modulus on every iteration and never succeeds. A single request of a few hundred bytes forces close to one CPU-second of work before an internal one-second watchdog kills the worker, and a larger modulus raises the cost further. By flooding such requests an attacker can saturate every scheduler and deny service, without credentials, a valid RSA key, or any special configuration.

This issue affects jose: from 1.7.7 before 1.11.13.

summary: Attacker-controlled AES-GCM authentication tag length allows tag forgery in jose
details:
## Summary

The pure-Erlang AES-GCM fallback in `jose_jwa_aes` derives the number of verified authentication tag bits from the attacker-supplied tag itself. In the `{aes_gcm, Bits}` clause of `block_decrypt/4`, the incoming tag is guarded only by `is_binary/1`, with no check on its length. Verification in `gcm_block_decrypt/6` then computes `TBits = bit_size(T)` and compares only those bits of the real 128-bit tag. An attacker who controls a JWE token can truncate the authentication tag to as little as 8 bits, so only 8 bits are ever checked. This reduces forgery resistance from 2^-128 to 2^-8, and a forged ciphertext is reliably accepted as authentic within 256 attempts without knowledge of the key (an authentication tag forgery and integrity bypass). Supplying a tag longer than 128 bits instead causes a badmatch that crashes the decrypting process. The fallback is reached through the public JWE decryption path whenever AES-GCM is not provided by a native crypto NIF, for example on FIPS or stripped or older OTP builds.

This issue affects jose: from 1.2.0 before 1.11.13.

## Workarounds

Ensure the runtime provides a crypto provider with native AES-GCM support (a standard Erlang/OTP build linked against OpenSSL) so that JOSE dispatches AES-GCM to the native `crypto` NIF instead of the `jose_jwa_aes` fallback.

## Configurations

This vulnerability is only exploitable when AES-GCM is handled by the pure-Erlang `jose_jwa_aes` fallback. That fallback is used on deployments where the Erlang/OTP `crypto` NIF does not expose native AES-GCM (for example FIPS builds, or stripped or older OTP releases). Deployments with a native AES-GCM crypto provider dispatch GCM through `crypto` and are not affected.

summary: XML comment injection in Saxy encoder via unescaped double hyphen
details:
## Summary

XML injection in the encoder of Saxy. `Saxy.Encoder` does not neutralize the `--` sequence in XML comment content: `escape_comment/2` returns the comment binary unchanged in every clause and only appends a space when the comment ends in a single `-`, so neither an interior `--` nor a full `-->` is escaped or rejected before the encoder wraps the content in the `<!--` and `-->` delimiters.

When an application serializes attacker-controlled text as a comment, through `Saxy.XML.comment/1` or a raw `{:comment, text}` simple form child, the attacker can close the comment early with `-->` and inject arbitrary sibling markup into the serialized document. A downstream parser then sees elements, attributes, and text that the application never built. Where the document is rendered as HTML or SVG, the injected markup executes as stored cross-site scripting; where it is consumed by another XML processor, the attacker can forge data that the producing application never emitted. Documents that Saxy only parses are not a vector.

This issue affects saxy: from 0.7.0 before 1.7.0.

## Workarounds

Reject or rewrite the `--` sequence in untrusted text before passing it to `Saxy.XML.comment/1`, for example by replacing `--` with `- -`.

Alternatively, stop emitting untrusted data as XML comments. Comments carry no semantic payload for consumers, so the text can usually be moved into an element or a CDATA section instead.

## Configurations

Only applications that place untrusted text into an XML comment node are affected. The untrusted value must reach `Saxy.XML.comment/1` or a raw `{:comment, text}` simple form child that is then serialized with `Saxy.encode!/2` or `Saxy.encode_to_iodata!/2`. Documents that are only parsed by Saxy never reach the encoder and are not a vector.

summary: Unsanitized URL schemes in MDEx Quill Delta output allow javascript: injection (XSS)
details: ## Summary Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation (XSS) vulnerability in leandrocp mdex allows cross-site scripting via unsanitized URL schemes in Quill Delta output. `MDEx.to_delta/2` converts Markdown into a Quill Delta. `MDEx.DeltaConverter.default_convert_node/3` in `lib/mdex/delta_converter.ex` copies the URL of a link, wikilink, or image node directly from the parsed Markdown into the Delta `"link"` or `"image"` attribute without applying a scheme allowlist or any normalization. An attacker who controls the Markdown text can supply a `javascript:` URL (for example `[click](javascript:alert(document.cookie))`) that survives verbatim into the Delta attribute. When the Delta is rendered to HTML by a downstream renderer (such as `quill-delta-to-html` or the Quill client), the attribute becomes an `` or ``, and the `javascript:` scheme executes in the browser of anyone who views the rendered content. The link and wikilink cases are the strongest vectors because `javascript:` in an `href` executes on click; the image case is lower impact because `javascript:` in `` generally does not execute in modern browsers. This issue affects mdex: from 0.8.3 before 0.13.2. ## Workarounds Sanitize the Quill Delta produced by `MDEx.to_delta/2` before rendering it: drop or blank any `"link"` or `"image"` value whose URL scheme is not in a safe allowlist (`http`, `https`, `mailto`, `tel`). ## Configurations The application must pass untrusted Markdown to `MDEx.to_delta/2` and then render the resulting Quill Delta to HTML with a renderer that maps the `"link"` and `"image"` attributes to `href` and `src` without applying its own URL scheme sanitization (for example `quill-delta-to-html` or the Quill client).

summary: mint buffers an entire chunked response chunk in memory in Mint.HTTP1.decode_body/5
details:
## Summary

Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling vulnerability in elixir-mint mint (`Mint.HTTP1` module) allows a denial of service via an oversized `chunked` transfer-encoded response.

This vulnerability is associated with program files `lib/mint/http1.ex` and program routines `Mint.HTTP1.decode_body/5`, `Mint.HTTP1.add_body_to_buffer/2`.

When Mint decodes a `chunked` HTTP response body, it accumulates each partial fragment of the current chunk in the connection's `data_buffer` (an unbounded iolist) via `add_body_to_buffer/2` and does not emit the data to the caller until the full declared chunk length has been received. The chunk size is taken directly from the server and parsed with no upper bound, so a malicious or compromised server can announce one enormous chunk (for example a size line of `7FFFFFFF`, about 2 GiB) and then send the body bytes slowly without ever completing the chunk. The client buffers every received byte while it waits for a completion that never arrives, and because no data responses are produced until the chunk finishes, a caller that otherwise streams large `content-length` bodies safely gains no protection. An unauthenticated remote server (reachable whenever a client follows redirects, fetches user-supplied URLs, or processes webhooks) can drive the client's memory arbitrarily high and trigger an out-of-memory condition.

This issue affects mint: from 0.5.0 before 1.9.1.

summary: Atom-table exhaustion denial of service in Guardian permissions AtomEncoding via unbounded atom creation
details:
## Summary

Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling in ueberauth guardian allows denial of service via unbounded atom creation from attacker-controlled binary input.

`Guardian.Permissions.AtomEncoding` encodes permission scopes by passing arbitrary binaries to `String.to_atom/1`. When `encode/3` in `lib/guardian/permissions/atom_encoding.ex` is called with a list, each binary entry is handled by the `encode_value/3` binary clause, which calls `String.to_atom(value)` with no allow-list check. The `perm_set` argument (the application's small, finite set of legitimate permission names) is discarded, so any external string flows straight into atom creation. This encoder is selected with `use Guardian.Permissions, encoding: Guardian.Permissions.AtomEncoding` and reached through the imported `encode/3` entry point.

`String.to_atom/1` creates a brand-new atom for every previously unseen binary, atoms are never garbage collected, and the BEAM atom table is fixed at roughly 1,048,576 entries by default. An application that funnels attacker-influenced permission scopes (from a request body, a JWT claim, or other external input) into `encode/3` therefore mints one permanent atom per distinct value. A modest stream of varied, unauthenticated input permanently consumes the atom table and crashes the BEAM node with `system_limit`, taking down every application running on it.

The default encoder is `Guardian.Permissions.BitwiseEncoding`, which is not affected.

This issue affects guardian: from 2.0.0 before 2.4.1.

## Workarounds

Switch the permission encoder to the default `Guardian.Permissions.BitwiseEncoding` or to `Guardian.Permissions.TextEncoding`, neither of which creates atoms. Alternatively, validate every permission value against the configured `perm_set` allowlist (rejecting unknown values) before passing it to `encode/3`.

## Configurations

Only applications that opt into the non-default `Guardian.Permissions.AtomEncoding` encoder (via `use Guardian.Permissions, encoding: Guardian.Permissions.AtomEncoding`) and pass attacker-influenced permission scopes into its `encode/3` entry point are exploitable. The default `Guardian.Permissions.BitwiseEncoding` encoder and the `Guardian.Permissions.TextEncoding` encoder do not create atoms and are not affected.

summary: Internal error terms inspected into AshTypescript RPC error responses
details:
## Summary

Generation of Error Message Containing Sensitive Information vulnerability in ash-project ash_typescript allows an unauthenticated attacker to read internal Elixir terms from an RPC error response by provoking an error the error builder has no dedicated clause for.

`AshTypescript.Rpc.ErrorBuilder.build_error_response/1` in `lib/ash_typescript/rpc/error_builder.ex` renders a pipeline error term that matches no specific clause with `inspect/1` and places the result in `details.error` of the client-facing error. Ash exceptions take a separate path in `AshTypescript.Rpc.Errors` where unhandled cases are redacted behind an `errorId`, but these fallbacks have no redaction, so whatever the term carries reaches the HTTP or channel response. Two request paths hand it such terms: a struct-typed action argument with an invalid nested value, where `cast_map_to_struct/2` in `lib/ash_typescript/rpc/input_formatter.ex` throws the raw `Ash.Type` cast error into the builder, and field selection on a generic action that returns a primitive, where `format_field_type/1` inspects the full `Ash.Info.Manifest.Type` struct into `vars.returnType`. Resource module names in `vars.resource` are not treated as sensitive and are out of scope.

This issue affects ash_typescript: from 0.1.0 before 0.19.1.

## Details

**1. Error funnel.** `AshTypescript.Rpc.run_action/3` runs the request through `Pipeline.parse_request/3`, `execute_ash_action/1` and `process_result/2`. Any `{:error, reason}` from these goes to `error_response/1`, which calls `AshTypescript.Rpc.ErrorBuilder.build_error_response/1` with the raw reason term.

**2. Unredacted fallbacks.** `build_error_response/1` has clauses for the error tuples the pipeline is expected to emit. A two-tuple whose first element is an atom but matches no clause is rendered as `field_validation_error` with `details.error` set to `inspect(error)`, and any other term becomes `unknown_error` with `details.error` set to `inspect(other)`. Ash exceptions never reach these clauses because `AshTypescript.Rpc.Errors` handles them and redacts unhandled ones behind an `errorId`, so only this path has no redaction.

**3. Reachable triggers.** `AshTypescript.Rpc.InputFormatter.cast_map_to_struct/2` throws the raw `Ash.Type.cast_input/3` error, a keyword list, when a struct-typed argument fails to cast, and `format/6` turns the throw into `{:error, term}` for the funnel. Separately, requesting `fields` on a generic action whose return type is a primitive produces an `{:invalid_field_selection, :primitive_type, return_type, ...}` tuple whose `return_type` is formatted by `format_field_type/1`, which inspects the whole `Ash.Info.Manifest.Type` struct, constraints and decoration included, into `vars.returnType`.

## Proof of concept

1. Expose an AshTypescript RPC action that takes a struct-typed argument, for example an `assignee` argument whose struct has a UUID `id` field.
2. Send the action request with an invalid nested value, such as `{"assignee": {"id": "not-a-uuid", "name": "x", "email": "e"}}`.
3. Read the response: each pair of the raw `Ash.Type` cast error is returned as its own `field_validation_error` with the inspected term in `details.error`.

For the second path, send a `fields` list to a generic action that returns a primitive and read the inspected `Ash.Info.Manifest.Type` struct in `vars.returnType` of the resulting error.

## Impact

Any client able to call the RPC endpoint can submit malformed struct arguments or field selections and read internal Elixir terms, including any state the failing pipeline step carried, from the error response.

## Configurations

The application exposes an AshTypescript RPC endpoint over HTTP or a channel and has an action with a struct-typed argument, or a generic action with a primitive return type that accepts field selection.

summary: HTTP/2 inbound flow control is not enforced, letting a client queue unbounded DATA in stream processes in Bandit
details:
## Summary

Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling vulnerability in the HTTP/2 implementation of mtrudel bandit allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to exhaust server memory via DATA frames sent past the advertised receive window. The attacker requests a response larger than the 65,535-byte initial window and withholds `WINDOW_UPDATE`, so the stream process blocks while sending and stops reading, then floods small DATA frames on that stream. Every frame is queued in the stream's mailbox until the BEAM node runs out of memory.

`Bandit.HTTP2.Connection.handle_frame/3` in `lib/bandit/http2/connection.ex` forwards each DATA frame to the stream process without consulting the receive window, and `Bandit.HTTP2.FlowControl.compute_recv_window/2` replenishes the window as data arrives rather than as it is consumed, and never answers a violation with `FLOW_CONTROL_ERROR`.

This issue affects bandit: from 0.3.1 before 1.14.0.

## Details

**1. Connection-level window** (`lib/bandit/http2/connection.ex`, `lib/bandit/http2/flow_control.ex`)

The `handle_frame/3` clause for DATA frames sends the payload to the stream process before any window is checked. It then calls `compute_recv_window/2`, which subtracts the frame size and, once the window drops below 2^30, advertises a `WINDOW_UPDATE` back up to 2^31-1. A negative window is accepted, so a peer that overruns the window is never refused, and the window refills when data arrives rather than when it is consumed.

**2. Stream-level window** (`lib/bandit/http2/stream.ex`)

The stream receive window is debited only when the stream process reads the DATA message, and it never rejects a violation either.

**3. Accumulation**

While `send_data/3` waits for send window, its selective `receive` matches only window updates and resets, so DATA messages pile up unread in the mailbox. A stream `WINDOW_UPDATE` of 1 byte, sent at intervals under the 15-second send timeout, keeps the stream alive while the attacker floods 1-byte DATA frames.

## Proof of concept

1. On an HTTP/2 connection, request a resource whose response exceeds 65,535 bytes and send no `WINDOW_UPDATE`. The server sends one window's worth and the stream blocks in `send_data/3`.
2. Send 1-byte DATA frames on that stream in batches, ignoring the server's receive windows.
3. Between batches, at intervals under 15 seconds, send a stream `WINDOW_UPDATE` with an increment of 1 to keep the blocked send alive.
4. Send a PING. It is acknowledged, and the server has sent neither `FLOW_CONTROL_ERROR` nor `GOAWAY` while its memory grows with every frame.

## Impact

An unauthenticated remote client can exhaust the memory of any Bandit server with HTTP/2 enabled by flooding DATA frames on a stream that is not reading its request body, such as one stalled sending a large response. The queued frames live in the BEAM node's memory, so exhausting it takes down every application on the node, not just the HTTP listener.

## Workarounds

From 0.7.0, disable HTTP/2 with `http_2_options: [enabled: false]`, which removes the vulnerable path.

summary: WebSocket sessions do not verify TLS certificates, exposing API keys and OAuth tokens to on-path attackers
details:
## Summary

Improper Certificate Validation vulnerability in the WebSocket streaming client in agentjido req_llm allows an on-path attacker to read and modify OpenAI WebSocket sessions, including the `authorization` bearer token, via a TLS certificate the client does not trust. `ReqLLM.Streaming.WebSocketSession.Client.start/3` in `lib/req_llm/streaming/web_socket_session/client.ex` starts WebSockex without TLS options, and WebSockex defaults to `insecure: true`, which connects with `verify: :verify_none`. The option allowlist also drops any caller-supplied `cacerts` or `ssl_options`, so an application cannot turn verification on.

The OpenAI Responses, Realtime, and Codex WebSocket paths reach this client and send the API key or OAuth access token in the `authorization` header. HTTP streaming through Finch and the HTTP/2 duplex session through Mint verify certificates and are not affected.

This issue affects req_llm: from 1.9.0 before 1.29.0.

## Details

**1. Entry points.** `ReqLLM.Providers.OpenAI.WebSocket.responses_url/2` and `realtime_url/2`, and the Codex provider's `codex_websocket_url/1`, turn the provider base URL into a `wss://` URL and start `ReqLLM.Streaming.WebSocketSession` with an `authorization` header that carries the OpenAI API key or the OAuth access token.

**2. Missing TLS options.** `WebSocketSession.init/1` passes only the headers and the timeouts to `WebSocketSession.Client.start/3`, and the allowlist in `start/3` forwards only `name`, `debug`, `async`, `handle_initial_conn_failure`, and the socket timeouts to `WebSockex.start/4`. No `insecure`, `cacerts`, or `ssl_options` value reaches WebSockex, and a caller cannot inject one.

**3. Insecure default.** WebSockex 0.5.1 sets `insecure: true` when the option is absent and opens the `wss://` connection through `:ssl.connect/4` with `verify: :verify_none`. Any certificate completes the handshake, so an attacker who terminates TLS on the path receives the upgrade request with the bearer token and every frame of the session, and can rewrite frames in either direction.

## Proof of concept

1. Start a TLS endpoint on `localhost` with a self-signed certificate chain that no trust store contains, and let it answer the WebSocket upgrade with `101 Switching Protocols`.
2. On a vulnerable version, call `ReqLLM.Streaming.WebSocketSession.start_link/2` with `wss://localhost:<port>/socket` and `headers: [{"authorization", "Bearer <token>"}]`, then `await_connected/2`.
3. `await_connected/2` returns `:ok`, the endpoint completes the TLS handshake, and the endpoint receives the upgrade request carrying the bearer token. On 1.29.0 the same call returns `{:error, %WebSockex.ConnError{original: {:tls_alert, {:unknown_ca, _}}}}` and the endpoint never sees the request.

## Impact

An attacker on the network path between an application and the OpenAI endpoint presents their own certificate, obtains the OpenAI API key or OAuth access token and the full session content, and can alter model output and tool calls before the application acts on them. Every application that uses the OpenAI Responses, Realtime, or Codex WebSocket paths is affected.

## Workarounds

Leave the `openai_stream_transport` provider option at its default `:sse` for the OpenAI and OpenAI Codex providers, and do not call `ReqLLM.Providers.OpenAI.WebSocket.start_responses_session/2` directly. Responses streaming then runs over HTTP through Finch, which verifies certificates. `ReqLLM.OpenAI.Realtime.connect/2` has no HTTP alternative, so do not use it on an affected version.

summary: Unvalidated HTTP/1 request-target authority lets a client choose conn.host and conn.port in Bandit
details:
## Summary

Improper Validation of Syntactic Correctness of Input vulnerability in mtrudel bandit allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to set `conn.host` and `conn.port` to values outside the RFC 3986 host grammar via the authority of an HTTP/1 absolute-form or authority-form request target. Bandit validates the `Host` header and answers 400 when it is malformed, but when the request target carries its own authority that authority takes precedence, as RFC 9112 requires, and `Bandit.Pipeline.determine_host_and_port!/4` in `lib/bandit/pipeline.ex` passes it to the application unchecked. A request line such as `GET http://good.example@evil.example/x HTTP/1.1` with a valid `Host` header yields a `conn.host` of `good.example@evil.example`, and the same path admits NUL, DEL and non-ASCII bytes, invalid IP literals and ports outside 1..65535. The HTTP/1.0 clause needs no `Host` header at all, and `CONNECT` places the unparsed port string in `conn.port`.

Applications that build absolute URLs from `conn.host`, such as through `Plug.Conn.request_url/1` or Phoenix URL helpers, emit links whose authority the attacker chose. Message framing is unaffected, and no CR or LF can reach `conn.host`.

This issue affects bandit: from 0.6.0 before 1.13.0.

## Details

**1. Request-target parsing** (`lib/bandit/http1/socket.ex`)

`:erlang.decode_packet/3` returns an absolute-form target as `{:absoluteURI, scheme, host, port, path}` and an authority-form (`CONNECT`) target as `{:scheme, host, port}`. `resolve_request_target!/2` unwraps both into a `{scheme, host, port, path}` tuple and forwards `host` and `port` as received. `validate_request_line!/2` only rejects bytes at or below `0x20` and `0x7F`, so userinfo, delimiters, backslashes, bytes `0x80` to `0xFF`, invalid IP literals and out-of-range ports pass. For `CONNECT`, `port` is the unparsed text after the first colon.

**2. Host selection** (`lib/bandit/pipeline.ex`)

`determine_host_and_port!/4` has three clauses. The HTTP/1.1 clause calls `required_host_header!/1`, which parses the `Host` header with `Bandit.Headers.parse_hostlike_header!/1` and raises a 400 on a malformed value, and then discards that result whenever `target_host` is set, returning `to_string(target_host)` and `target_port` instead. The fallback clause used for HTTP/1.0 and for `CONNECT` returns the target host and port directly and never consults the `Host` header. The precedence itself follows RFC 9112 section 3.2.2; the defect is that the value which wins is the one never validated.

**3. Effect**

`build_conn!/6` places the pair into the `URI` from which `Plug.Conn.Adapter.conn/5` builds `conn.host` and `conn.port`. The application therefore sees host values Bandit rejects on every other route into the same field, and for `CONNECT` a binary where `Plug.Conn.port_number/0` promises an integer, which makes `Plug.Conn.request_url/1` raise.

## Proof of concept

1. Start Bandit over plaintext HTTP with a plug that returns `conn.host` and `conn.port`.
2. Open a raw TCP connection to the listener and send `GET http://good.example@evil.example/x HTTP/1.1` followed by `Host: good.example` and an empty line. The response is 200 and `conn.host` is `good.example@evil.example`.
3. Repeat with `GET http://ex\x00am.com/x HTTP/1.1` (a NUL byte in the authority) or `GET http://ex.com:99999/x HTTP/1.1`. Both are accepted, with the NUL byte in `conn.host` and 99999 in `conn.port`.
4. Send the same bytes in the `Host` header of an origin-form request instead. Bandit answers 400 for the NUL byte and the out-of-range port on 1.12.5, and for every payload once the `Host` grammar tightening on main is released.
5. Send `GET http://good.example@evil.example/x HTTP/1.0` with no `Host` header, or `CONNECT good.example@evil.example:443 HTTP/1.1`. Both are accepted, and the `CONNECT` form leaves `conn.port` as the binary `"443"`.

## Impact

An unauthenticated client can make the application see any host string and any port number as the request's authority, bypassing the validation applied to the `Host` header. An application that builds absolute URLs from `conn.host`, such as password-reset or verification links, emits links whose host the attacker chose.

## Workarounds

Add a plug ahead of any code that reads `conn.host` or `conn.port` that compares `conn.host` against an allow-list of the hostnames the application serves, checks that `conn.port` is an integer, and halts the request with a 400 response otherwise. Do not derive absolute URLs from `conn.host` until that check has passed.

summary: Query-complexity limit bypass via first/last pagination arguments in AshGraphql enables denial of service
details:
## Summary

Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling vulnerability in ash-project ash_graphql allows an unauthenticated client to bypass the configured GraphQL query-complexity limit and force an unbounded database read.

`AshGraphql.Graphql.Resolver.query_complexity/3` multiplies child complexity by the requested page size only when the argument map contains `:limit` (offset pagination). Relay connections and keyset pagination use `first` and `last`, which never match that clause and fall through to the catch-all that returns `child_complexity + 1`. A nested relay query such as `posts(first: 500) { edges { node { comments(first: 500) { ... } } } }` therefore scores as trivially cheap while materializing the full fan-out, passing an Absinthe `max_complexity` cap that rejects the equivalent `limit`-based query. The fix adds `first` and `last` clauses clamped to the action's page size.

This issue affects ash_graphql: from 0.16.23 before 1.11.0.

summary: Match regex runs on over-length input in Ash.Type.String, enabling regex denial of service
details:
## Summary

Uncontrolled Resource Consumption vulnerability in ash-project ash allows an attacker to force an expensive regular expression to run on input that a length constraint should have already rejected.

`Ash.Type.String.apply_constraints/2` (`lib/ash/type/string.ex`) evaluated the `:match` regex regardless of the `min_length` and `max_length` constraints on the same attribute. Because the length check did not gate the regex, an over-length value that the length constraint rejects still had the pattern applied to it, so the length limit that would otherwise bound the work never constrained the regex input. Against a backtracking pattern this yields catastrophic regex evaluation on attacker-sized input, and even a linear pattern runs on arbitrarily large input, consuming CPU per request. The fix skips the `:match` regex whenever a length constraint is violated, making the two checks order-independent.

This issue affects ash: from 0.10.0 before 3.32.2.

summary: Unvalidated object metadata in ex_aws_s3 enables HTTP header (CRLF) injection into S3 requests
details:
## Summary

ex_aws_s3 builds `x-amz-meta-*` request headers by interpolating user-supplied object metadata directly into header names and values without any validation. In `ExAws.S3.Utils.build_meta_headers/1` (`lib/ex_aws/s3/utils.ex`), each `:meta` entry is turned into a header as `{"x-amz-meta-#{k}", v}` with no check for carriage return (CR), line feed (LF), or other illegal header bytes.

Object metadata is routinely derived from end-user input (for example an upload service that lets users attach a comment or label to an object). When such input reaches `ExAws.S3.put_object/4` or any other operation accepting the `:meta` option, a value containing CR/LF is carried unchanged into the outbound header list. If the configured HTTP adapter does not neutralize header values before writing them to the socket, the embedded CRLF starts a new header line, allowing an attacker to inject arbitrary headers into (or split) the HTTP request the library sends to the S3 endpoint. This is an HTTP header (CRLF) injection leading to HTTP request splitting. The practical impact depends on the HTTP adapter, and no authentication is required beyond the ability to influence object metadata.

This issue affects ex_aws_s3: from 2.0.0 before 2.6.0.

## Details

**1. Unvalidated header construction.** `ExAws.S3.Utils.build_meta_headers/1` in `lib/ex_aws/s3/utils.ex` turns each `:meta` entry into `{"x-amz-meta-#{k}", v}`. Neither the key nor the value is checked for CR, LF or other illegal header bytes.

**2. Untrusted metadata.** Object metadata is routinely populated from end-user input, such as a comment or label attached to an upload. A value like `"legit\r\nX-Injected-By-Attacker: pwned"` reaches the header list unchanged through `ExAws.S3.put_object/4` or any operation taking `:meta`.

**3. Header injection.** If the HTTP adapter does not validate header values before writing them to the socket, the embedded CRLF ends the `x-amz-meta-*` line and starts a new one, injecting arbitrary headers into, or splitting, the request sent to S3. The library delegates this safety to the adapter entirely.

## Proof of concept

1. An upload service forwards user-supplied metadata: `ExAws.S3.put_object("victim-bucket", "uploads/file.txt", "hello", meta: [{"comment", value}])`.
2. The attacker sets the value to `legit\r\nX-Injected-By-Attacker: pwned\r\nX-Smuggled: yes`.
3. `build_meta_headers/1` copies it verbatim into the `x-amz-meta-comment` header.
4. With an adapter that does not reject CR/LF, the bytes on the wire contain `X-Injected-By-Attacker: pwned` and `X-Smuggled: yes` as separate header lines.

## Impact

This is an HTTP header (CRLF) injection / request-splitting issue. Anyone using `ex_aws_s3` to store objects whose metadata is derived from untrusted input (upload services, multi-tenant file stores, anything exposing object metadata over an HTTP boundary) is affected. The practical impact depends on the configured HTTP adapter: adapters that validate header values will reject or strip the injection, but the library offers no guarantee and performs no validation of its own, so the safety of the request is silently delegated to the HTTP client.

## Workarounds

Reject or strip carriage return (CR) and line feed (LF) characters from object metadata keys and values before passing them to ex_aws_s3, or configure an HTTP adapter that neutralizes CR/LF in header values before writing them to the socket (for example hackney 4.x).

## Configurations

The vulnerability is only exploitable when an application both populates object `:meta` entries from untrusted input and uses an HTTP adapter that does not neutralize CR/LF in header values before writing them to the socket. The default adapter (hackney 4.x) strips CR/LF from header values, which masks the issue; the library performs no validation of its own and silently delegates safety to the configured HTTP client.

summary: Ash.Type ignores outer array constraints on nested {:array, {:array, type}} inputs
details:
## Summary

Improper Input Validation vulnerability in ash-project ash fails to enforce the outer array constraints on a doubly-nested `{:array, {:array, type}}` attribute, letting invalid input pass validation.

`Ash.Type.apply_constraints/3` (`lib/ash/type/type.ex`) handled the `{:array, {:array, type}}` case by mapping only the inner `{:array, type}` constraints over each element, so constraints declared on the outer array (such as `min_length`, `max_length`, and `nil_items?`) were never applied. An attacker could submit an outer list that violates those constraints (too many elements, or `nil` entries where disallowed) and have it accepted and persisted. The fix enforces the outer array constraints and adds explicit handling for `nil` and non-list inputs.

This issue affects ash: from 2.16.1 before 3.32.2.

summary: Ash.Resource.Validation.Confirm leaks a confirmed field's stored value in the atomic mismatch error
details:
## Summary

Generation of Error Message Containing Sensitive Information vulnerability in ash-project ash discloses the stored value of a confirmed field to an actor who fails its confirmation check.

`Ash.Resource.Validation.Confirm`'s atomic implementation (`atomic/2` in `lib/ash/resource/validation/confirm.ex`) built the mismatch error with its `value` set to the field being confirmed. When the actor supplies only the confirmation argument and not the field itself, `value` resolves through `atomic_ref/2` to the field's current stored value, so the mismatch error echoes that stored value back to the actor. Against a confirmation guarding a sensitive attribute, an actor can submit a deliberately wrong confirmation and read the real value from the returned error. The fix reports the actor-supplied confirmation in the error instead of the stored field value.

This issue affects ash: from 2.17.20 before 3.32.2.

summary: Unescaped path parameters in AshTypescript generated TypeScript client allow request redirection
details:
## Summary

URL Redirection to Untrusted Site ('Open Redirect') vulnerability in ash-project ash_typescript allows an attacker who controls a path-parameter value to redirect a generated client's request, and the credentials attached to it, to an unintended route or an external origin.

The URL builders in `lib/ash_typescript/typed_controller/codegen/route_renderer.ex` replace each `:param` placeholder with a bare template interpolation and never call `encodeURIComponent`, so the value reaches `executeTypedControllerRequest` raw. A value containing `../` is normalised away by the fetch URL resolver and reaches a different route, while `?` or `#` truncates the path and can smuggle or override query parameters. For a route whose path begins with a parameter, a value such as `/evil.example.com/x` yields the protocol-relative URL `//evil.example.com/x`, sending the request and the credentials from `TypedControllerConfig` to an attacker-controlled host. Nothing constrains the value at runtime: `get_path_param_type/2` emits only a TypeScript type, which is erased.

The query-string path is unaffected, since `URLSearchParams.set` encodes its own values.

This issue affects ash_typescript: from 0.15.0 before 0.18.0.

## Configurations

The application ships a TypeScript client generated by AshTypescript for a typed-controller route taking a path parameter, and passes untrusted input as that parameter.

summary: Revoked session accepted because the session jti is never checked in AshAuthentication and AshAuthentication Phoenix
details:
## Summary

Insufficient Session Expiration vulnerability in team-alembic AshAuthentication and AshAuthentication Phoenix allows a revoked session to remain fully authenticated.

A resource configured with `session_identifier :jti` and `require_token_presence_for_authentication?` disabled stores its session value as `<jti>:<subject>`. The `jti` is there so that signing out can revoke that one session. Neither reader consults it: `AshAuthentication.Plug.Helpers.authenticate_resource_from_session/4` and `AshAuthentication.Phoenix.LiveSession.on_mount/4` both split the value with `split_identifier/2`, discard the `jti` and pass the bare subject to `AshAuthentication.subject_to_user/3`, which reloads the record. The token-presence branch of each function does check its token, calling `AshAuthentication.TokenResource.Actions.get_token/3` with the `jti` and the purpose `user`. Because the revocation record is never read, neither its revoked state nor its expiry constrains the session, so a session captured before sign-out keeps working.

This issue affects ash_authentication: from 4.9.1 before 4.15.0 and from 5.0.0-rc.0 before 5.0.0-rc.14; ash_authentication_phoenix: from 2.10.0 before 2.17.4 and from 3.0.0-rc.0 before 3.0.0-rc.11.

summary: ash_authentication_oauth2_server interpolates a tenant-derived value into the WWW-Authenticate challenge without escaping, allowing header parameter injection
details:
## Summary

Improper Encoding or Escaping of Output vulnerability in ash-project ash_authentication_oauth2_server allows an unauthenticated attacker to inject arbitrary authentication parameters into the `WWW-Authenticate` challenge header.

`BearerPlug` and `RequireScopePlug` built the `Bearer resource_metadata="..."` challenge by interpolating a `resource_metadata` URL derived from the request tenant directly into the quoted value. In a multi-tenant application that sets the Ash tenant from request-controlled data (a subdomain, the `Host`, a path segment, or a header), a tenant containing a `"` closes the quoted value and appends attacker-chosen auth-params, including a second `resource_metadata` URL pointing at an attacker-controlled authorization server that spec-following clients follow. Carriage returns and line feeds are rejected by Plug, so this is parameter injection within one header, not response splitting.

This issue affects ash_authentication_oauth2_server: from 0.1.3 before 0.3.1.

## Configurations

Reachable only in a multi-tenant application that derives the Ash tenant from request-controlled input (subdomain, `Host`, path, or header) and uses `BearerPlug` or `RequireScopePlug`; the tenant reaches the challenge through the server's tenant-aware `resource_url`.

summary: Unbounded atom creation from client-supplied RPC field names in AshTypescript field formatter
details:
## Summary

Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling vulnerability in ash-project ash_typescript allows an unauthenticated attacker to exhaust the BEAM atom table and abort the node via client-supplied RPC field names.

`AshTypescript.FieldFormatter.convert_to_field_atom/2` in `lib/ash_typescript/field_formatter.ex` converts a client-supplied field name to an atom with `String.to_atom/1` when no matching atom already exists. It delegates first to `parse_input_field/2`, which resolves the name with `String.to_existing_atom/1` and falls back to returning the plain string; `convert_to_field_atom/2` then mints an atom from that string rather than treating the name as unknown.

RPC field selection reaches it for every requested field name through `AshTypescript.Rpc.FieldProcessing.FieldSelector`, which resolves each name before checking that the field exists, with no allowlist, length bound, or rate limit. Atoms are never garbage collected, so each distinct name mints a permanent one and the VM aborts once the atom table limit is reached. A field name over 255 characters additionally raises an uncaught `SystemLimitError`.

This issue affects ash_typescript: from 0.1.0 before 0.18.0.

## Configurations

The application exposes an AshTypescript RPC endpoint over HTTP, so that client-supplied field names reach `AshTypescript.Rpc.run_action/3`.

summary: HTTP/2 header field values containing CR, LF or NUL are passed to the application unvalidated in Bandit
details:
## Summary

Improper Neutralization of CRLF Sequences ('CRLF Injection') vulnerability in mtrudel bandit allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to smuggle CR, LF, or NUL characters into application-visible request headers via HTTP/2. `Bandit.HTTP2.Stream.read_headers/1` validates pseudo-header placement and uniqueness, header-name casing, connection-specific headers, the `te` value, and `content-length`, but never checks field *values*. Because HPACK carries arbitrary octets, a HEADERS block whose field values contain `\r`, `\n`, or `\0` decodes without error and the values land in `conn.req_headers` unchanged. The HTTP/1 path already rejects the same octets; HTTP/2 did not.

Bandit itself is not a sink for the injected bytes: its own logging uses fixed strings or `inspect`, and HTTP/2 response headers are HPACK-encoded and separately rejected by Plug's `put_resp_header`, so response splitting is not reachable through this path. The risk is entirely in how a downstream application consumes header values, such as appending one verbatim to a plain-text log or concatenating it into an upstream request. A related gap bundled in the same fix: only `:method`, `:scheme`, and `:path` were checked for at most one occurrence; a duplicate `:authority` pseudo-header was accepted, with the first instance silently winning as `conn.host` while a conflicting value remained visible to the application.

This issue affects bandit: from 1.4.0 before 1.12.5.

summary: YAML injection via unescaped newlines in ymlr document comments
details:
## Summary

Improper Neutralization of CRLF Sequences vulnerability in ufirstgroup ymlr (`Ymlr` module) allows attackers to inject arbitrary content into generated YAML documents through document comments. `Ymlr.document!/2` interpolates each caller-supplied comment string into the output behind a single `#` prefix without validating it or escaping line breaks. Because a YAML comment is terminated by a line break, the first carriage return or line feed in the comment string ends the comment context and everything after it is emitted at column 0 of the document body.

An attacker who controls text that the host application passes as a comment can forge top-level mapping keys, override values the application itself set, and emit `---` or `...` markers that split the output into additional documents. Downstream consumers of the generated YAML, such as configuration loaders, deployment manifests, CI pipelines and data importers, parse the injected content as legitimate data. The same clause backs `Ymlr.document/2`, `Ymlr.documents!/2` and `Ymlr.documents/2`, so every document encoding entry point is affected.

This vulnerability is associated with program files `lib/ymlr.ex` and program routines `Ymlr.document!/2`, `Ymlr.documents!/2`.

This issue affects ymlr: from 0.0.1 before 5.1.6.

## Workarounds

Split any untrusted comment string on line breaks and pass the resulting list as the comment element of the `{comment, data}` tuple. Ymlr prefixes every list element with its own `#` marker, so no line can leave the comment context. Alternatively, reject comment strings that contain carriage return or line feed characters, or keep untrusted text out of comments entirely and place it in the encoded data instead, where the encoder quotes it.

## Configurations

A deployment is vulnerable when the host application places attacker-controlled text in the comment position of a document, that is, as the first element of the `{comment, data}` tuple passed to `Ymlr.document!/2`, `Ymlr.document/2`, `Ymlr.documents!/2` or `Ymlr.documents/2`. Callers that encode data without comments, or that use only static comment strings, are not exploitable.

summary: Cowboy HTTP/1.1 max_headers Bypass via Duplicate Header Names Enables Memory Exhaustion
details:
## Summary

Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling vulnerability in ninenines cowboy allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to exhaust connection process memory over HTTP/1.1.

The HTTP/1.1 handler in `cowboy_http` enforces the `max_headers` limit by counting the number of distinct header names in a map (`maps:size(Headers)`). When a request contains multiple header lines with the same name, the values are concatenated into a single ever-growing binary stored under that one map key (`", "` for regular headers, `"; "` for cookies), so the map size stays at one and the `max_headers` cap (default 100) is never reached. Because no accumulator bounds the total number of header lines or the total byte size of the header block (only per-line `max_header_name_length` and `max_header_value_length` apply), an unauthenticated client can send an arbitrary number of header lines with the same name and grow the connection process's binary memory to arbitrary size within the request window.

The impact per connection is bounded by `request_timeout` (default 5 seconds, not reset by header data), and by `max_heap_size` when set (the offending connection process is killed once its heap grows past the limit). When `max_heap_size` is left at the default (unset), sustained abuse can drive the Erlang VM into out-of-memory conditions.

This issue affects cowboy: from 2.0.0-pre.4 before 2.18.0.

summary: ex_aws_ses missing URI-encoding of list_name allows path injection into SES V2 request URLs
details:
## Summary

Improper Encoding or Escaping of Output vulnerability in ex-aws ex_aws_ses (`ExAws.SES` module) allows path injection into Amazon SES V2 request URLs.

This vulnerability is associated with program file `lib/ex_aws/ses.ex` and program routines `ExAws.SES.delete_contact_list/1`, `ExAws.SES.get_contact_list/1`, `ExAws.SES.update_contact_list/2`, `ExAws.SES.create_contact/3`, `ExAws.SES.get_contact/2`, `ExAws.SES.update_contact/3`, `ExAws.SES.delete_contact/2` and `ExAws.SES.list_contacts/1`.

The V2 contact-list and contact functions interpolate the caller-supplied `list_name` into the request path without URI-encoding it, unlike the email address in the same functions which is passed through `ExAws.Request.Url.uri_encode/1`. An application that forwards untrusted input as a contact-list name lets an attacker embed `/`, `..` or `?` to escape the intended `contact-lists/<name>` path segment. A value such as `x/../suppression/addresses/victim%40example.com` makes a `delete_contact_list/1` call arrive at the account-wide suppression list. The request is still signed with the application's own AWS credentials and sent to the configured SES host, so the impact is cross-resource request forgery inside the caller's own AWS account, not arbitrary SSRF. Applications that only use hardcoded or strictly validated list names are not affected.

This issue affects ex_aws_ses: from 2.3.0 before 2.5.0.

## Details

**1. Raw interpolation.** Every V2 contact-list and contact function in `lib/ex_aws/ses.ex` builds its resource string by interpolating `list_name` as given, for example `request_v2(:delete, "contact-lists/#{list_name}")` in `delete_contact_list/1`. `request_v2/2` then appends it to the operation path as `@v2_path <> "/#{resource}"`.

**2. Inconsistent encoding.** The same functions pass the email address through `ExAws.Request.Url.uri_encode/1`, but `list_name` is neither encoded nor validated. `uri_encode/1` itself leaves `/` unencoded, so an email address containing `/` can add path segments as well.

**3. Segment escape.** A list name such as `x/../suppression/addresses/victim%40example.com` produces `/v2/email/contact-lists/x/../suppression/addresses/victim%40example.com`, which normalizes to the account's suppression list. Appending `/contacts/<addr>` turns a list-level operation into a contact operation, and a `?` can inject query parameters. The request is signed with the application's credentials and sent to the configured SES host, so the effect is cross-resource request forgery inside the caller's own AWS account.

## Proof of concept

1. An application takes a contact-list name from untrusted input and calls `ExAws.SES.delete_contact_list(list_name) |> ExAws.request()`.
2. The attacker supplies `x/../suppression/addresses/victim@example.com` (with the `@` percent-encoded) as the list name.
3. `delete_contact_list/1` interpolates it unencoded, so the signed request is `DELETE /v2/email/contact-lists/x/../suppression/addresses/victim%40example.com`.
4. Once the `..` is normalized, the request deletes the victim address from the account-wide suppression list instead of deleting a contact list.

## Impact

An attacker who controls a contact-list name, or an email address passed to the V2 contact functions, can redirect an authenticated, SigV4-signed SES request to a different resource in the account, causing unintended reads, modifications or deletions (for example manipulating the account-wide suppression list) while the application believes it is operating only on the named contact list or contact. Applications that only use hardcoded or strictly validated values for these arguments are not affected.

## Workarounds

Restrict `list_name` to Amazon SES's permitted contact-list character set, or run it through `ExAws.Request.Url.uri_encode/1`, before passing it to the affected functions.

## Configurations

The application must pass externally-influenced input (such as an HTTP parameter, a queue message, or a tenant record) as the `list_name` argument to one of the affected `ExAws.SES` V2 contact-list or contact functions. Applications that only use hardcoded or strictly validated list names are not affected.

summary: Quadratic CPU blow-up reassembling fragmented WebSocket messages in Bandit
details:
## Summary

Inefficient Algorithmic Complexity vulnerability in mtrudel bandit allows unauthenticated remote denial of service via CPU exhaustion during WebSocket fragment reassembly.

The size guard `Bandit.WebSocket.Connection.oversize_message?/2` called from `handle_frame/3` in `lib/bandit/websocket/connection.ex` appends each non-final continuation frame to a left-nested iolist and then re-measures the entire accumulated buffer with `IO.iodata_length/1` on every frame. Because the buffer grows by one element per frame and is fully re-traversed each time, reassembly work is quadratic (O(n^2)) in the number of continuation frames.

The `max_fragmented_message_size` limit (default 8 MB) bounds total bytes but not frame count, and each frame can carry as little as one payload byte, so an attacker can send millions of tiny continuation frames using modest bandwidth to pin a CPU core for minutes to hours. Many concurrent connections can starve the whole server of CPU, denying service to legitimate users. The WebSocket read timeout does not help, because it is an idle timeout evaluated between reads and cannot preempt the synchronous reassembly work spent inside a single callback.

This issue affects bandit: from 1.11.0 before 1.12.1.

## Configurations

This vulnerability only affects applications that serve WebSocket endpoints through Bandit (including Phoenix applications that use Bandit as the HTTP adapter). Applications that do not upgrade any connections to WebSocket are not affected.

summary: CDATA Section Breakout via Unsanitised ]]> in xml_builder
details:
## Summary

XML Injection vulnerability in joshnuss xml_builder (`XmlBuilder` module) allows Content Spoofing, XML Injection.

This vulnerability is associated with program files `lib/xml_builder.ex` and program routines `XmlBuilder.generate/1`, `XmlBuilder.generate/2`, `XmlBuilder.escape/1`.

The `escape/1` clause for `{:cdata, data}` in `lib/xml_builder.ex` concatenates data verbatim between the CDATA opener `<![CDATA[` and closer `]]>` without rewriting or splitting on the embedded `]]>` sequence. Because CDATA sections have no internal escape mechanism, the only safe way to embed arbitrary bytes is to split on `]]>` and emit adjacent CDATA sections. An attacker who can supply input containing `]]>` closes the CDATA section early; any bytes that follow are parsed as ordinary XML markup by downstream consumers, allowing injection of arbitrary elements, text, or entity references into the output document.

This issue affects xml_builder: from 0.0.7 before 2.4.1.

summary: Unbounded atom creation while parsing SAML messages in esaml allows atom table exhaustion
details:
## Summary

Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling vulnerability in `esaml_binding` in dropbox esaml allows an unauthenticated attacker to exhaust the Erlang VM atom table and crash the node via a crafted `SAMLResponse`.

`esaml_binding:decode_response/2` parses the decoded `SAMLResponse` with `xmerl_scan:string/2`, which interns every element name, attribute name, and namespace prefix it reads as a permanent atom. The SAML consume (ACS) and single-logout endpoints call it on unauthenticated requests before any signature check, so one well-formed document with thousands of distinct names mints thousands of atoms while staying inside the 128 KB request body limit. Atoms are never reclaimed and the VM caps the atom table at about one million entries, so a few dozen requests abort the node.

This issue affects esaml: from 0.1.0 onward.

## Details

**1. Input.** The SAML consume (ACS) and single-logout endpoints in `esaml_cowboy` read the request body, capped at 128 KB, and pass the `SAMLResponse` form field to `esaml_binding:decode_response/2`. Both the DEFLATE clause and the default clause end in `xmerl_scan:string/2` with `namespace_conformant` set.

**2.
